predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded for whether the reservation field is named, against what the agent actually changed. **The prediction is deliberately harsh and its failure would be good news.** A cohort that expects an agent to reach for concurrency settings and retries rather than for the accounting has a working model of where an agent's attention goes, and that model is what [S077](/wiki/seminars/S077.md) will require four quarters later.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Across the cohort, the truncation rate reported at step 3 will be near zero under the current discipline and will rise materially under whichever discipline each student chooses at step 5.
predictions.instrument: paired truncation rates before and after, per class. **This is §8 objection 1's repair reporting on itself.** If the rate does not rise, the recovery was free and the objection was wrong; if it rises and nobody mentions it in the step 5 justification, the fail condition is doing the work the objection said was needed.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 2, a majority will name a number and omit an owner.
predictions.instrument: item 2 responses coded for the presence of a named owner. **This is the day's cleanest evidence for point 1 and it is taken before any instruction**; if a majority do name owners, the day's central distinction is already held and phase 3's construction is over-built.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Situation D will be misclassified as a capacity event by more than half the cohort, and situation C will be classified correctly by more than half but will produce the largest number of unprompted written comments.
predictions.instrument: phase 3 classifications coded per situation, with free-text volume recorded per situation. **The split is the claim: D is the cognitive payload and C is the affective one, and the design predicts they will not be the same case.**

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Items 3 and 4 will show more constraints predicted movable than the same students predicted at S039, and the increase will be concentrated on the commercial constraints rather than the technical ones.
predictions.instrument: items 3 and 4 against the same students' S039 items 1 and 4, coded by constraint type. **If the increase is uniform across both types, the cohort has become generally more optimistic rather than having learned that commercial constraints have purposes**, which is a different and less useful outcome.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Fewer than one in six recommendations at step 7 will be *do not proceed* or *proceed under a named condition that is not met*.
predictions.instrument: step 7 recommendations coded by direction, with the evidence quality coded independently. **If the refusal rate is near zero while evidence quality is high, the specification's explicit permission is not being believed**, and the countermeasure — stating it in writing — has failed at the first day it was tried.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At phase 3's second closing task, the routing-error rate will be highest for situation C and lowest for situation A, and the modal error on C will be to name a technical owner.
predictions.instrument: the phase 3 routing answers coded per situation against the correct party. **This is the instrument objection 1's repair created and the day previously did not have.** The predicted pattern is point 8's claim stated as a measurement: engineers route commercially-caused failures technically, and C is the situation with no technical cause at all.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Fewer than one in five item 5 sealed predictions will name a *party* the agent fails to consult, while a majority will name a *quantity* it assumes.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded into the two categories, against what the agent produced. **The gap between the two rates is the module's frontier finding.** A cohort that predicts an agent will assume capacity it does not have is reasoning about the agent's knowledge; a cohort that predicts it will not ask the signatory is reasoning about the agent's position in an organisation, which is the harder model and the one point 8 requires.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: The modal awarded level will be 2b, and among sub-2b awards the modal cited failure condition will be the second — fitting the budget by silently accepting an untold degradation — rather than the first.
predictions.instrument: awarded levels coded against the five published failure conditions. **The direction is the claim**: under-asking reads as prudence and the cohort will import it from everywhere else they have been.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Fewer than half the cohort will produce two materially different arguments; most will deliver one argument twice with the vocabulary adjusted.
predictions.instrument: the two encounters coded independently by the assessors, before the defence, for material difference in what was selected. **If most deliver one argument twice, the competence [WP-013](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-013.md) named as assessed here is not being produced, and the two-payer construction is doing less than §3.3 claims.**

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Assessor divergence will be low on artefacts that fail a published failure condition and high on artefacts that pass all five.
predictions.instrument: independent pre-conferral levels, with the divergence rate reported against failure-condition status. **This is §8 objection 2's test.** The predicted pattern is the signature of a level anchored on inspection where inspection is available and unmanaged where it is not; the contrary result — divergence roughly equal in both groups — would show the checklist is not doing the anchoring.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Category 3 at phase 5 will be dominated by costs the [S061](/wiki/seminars/S061.md) scope statement had already named as omitted, rather than by costs nobody named.
predictions.instrument: category 3 items coded named against unnamed, per [WP-061](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-061.md) §9 prediction 4. **The two results call for different repairs**: unnamed omissions indicate a modelling failure at S061, and named omissions indicate a scope statement that was delivered, understood, and not acted on — which is the failure the strong form of the scope rule was adopted to prevent and would be evidence that the strong form is not sufficient on its own.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of item 5 sealed predictions will state that the agent's draft ask omits something, and fewer than one in five will name the refusal branch specifically.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded for which of the three omissions — owner, expiry, refusal branch — is named, against the agent's actual output. **The refusal branch is the prediction.** An owner and an expiry are elements of a specification the cohort has been drilled on; a prepared answer to *what if I say no* is a professional posture rather than an artefact element, and it is the one thing on this day that no specification anywhere in the programme has ever required. If a substantial number name it, the posture has formed without being taught, which would be the most encouraging single result in the module.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Assessor divergence on artefacts passing all five failure conditions will be higher for students whose appended intervention records are short than for those whose records are long, controlling for encounter quality as coded independently.
predictions.instrument: pre-conferral level divergence against appended-record length, with encounter quality coded blind. **This is §8 objection 4's test and it is the only one available.** A relationship in either direction is evidence that the records are being read into the judgement; no relationship is evidence that the declared separation holds, and would be the first empirical support this design has for a firewall it asserts in several places.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 2, fewer than a quarter of students will name the false-block error unprompted, and those who do will be disproportionately students with professional release experience.
predictions.instrument: item 2 enumerations coded for both error classes, split by the admission background survey. **This is the day's founding claim and the prediction it most needs to survive**; if half the cohort names it, point 2 is not the day's content and phase 4's weighting is wrong.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 3, more than half of students will read the fourteen-month clean record as evidence about the changes rather than about the gate, and fewer than one in five will reach the third reading.
predictions.instrument: item 3 responses coded into the three readings.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Groups will rank G4 last, and the ranking will be near-unanimous.
predictions.instrument: phase 3 committed rankings. **If a majority ranks G4 first, the payload has been anticipated** and the fallback question in §5 becomes the phase's content rather than its reserve.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: More than half of step 3 submissions will state the false-block rate as unmeasured and describe what would be needed, rather than inventing a figure — and the proportion that invent one will be higher among students who ranked G4 last most confidently.
predictions.instrument: step 3 submissions coded for invented, honestly-absent, or evidenced, cross-tabulated against phase 3 rankings. **The cross-tabulation is the claim**: confidence in a written gate and willingness to invent its error rate should not be related, and the design predicts they are.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 5, a large majority will predict that the agent's pipeline contains an error, and fewer than one in five will predict that its failure will be an accepted default or an absent failure condition rather than a defect.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded into defect-predicted and decision-predicted, against what each student's agent actually produced. **The gap between the two rates is this day's frontier-calibration measure.** If the decision-predicted rate is high, the cohort already holds the day's central distinction and points 9 and 10 are consolidation rather than content; if both rates are low, students are not yet predicting agent behaviour at all and the sealed item is measuring nothing.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: Across the three forced decisions at step 5, the threshold will be changed most often and the conversation split least often, and the split will be changed by fewer than a third of students even though phase 3 ran the comparison in front of them.
predictions.instrument: step 5 decision records coded by setting and by whether the recorded reason cites the phase 3 result. **This is the day's test of whether an executed contrasting case transfers into an artefact decision forty minutes later.** If the split rate is high, phase 3's executed payload is doing the work the design claims; if it is low while the threshold rate is high, students are changing the setting they were told about rather than the one they measured.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 2, more than three-quarters of students will name population as the single most likely reason, and item 3's opposite-direction case will be explained by a majority with a second mechanism rather than by revising the first.
predictions.instrument: item 2 responses coded against the five differences; item 3 responses coded for whether the student revised or added. **The add-versus-revise split is the claim**: adding indicates a frame forming, revising indicates a single-cause model defending itself.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At step 5, more than half of students will construct a class that is not in the substrate's taxonomy, and the classes will cluster on access path and device rather than on any content property.
predictions.instrument: constructed classes coded for taxonomy membership and for defining dimension. **If most constructed classes turn out to be recoverable from existing dimensions, O3's second surprise did not transfer** and step 5 is being performed as a slicing exercise.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Step 3's pre-committed dominant difference will match step 6's attribution for fewer than half of students, and the largest off-diagonal cell will be predicted-population against attributed-criterion.
predictions.instrument: the step 3 by step 6 matrix.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: The [S049](/wiki/seminars/S049.md) found-factor rate will be higher online than it was offline — partners will find more omitted clustering factors when the unit is a user.
predictions.instrument: the two found-factor rates, paired by student. **If the online rate is not higher, either the checklist transferred completely or the online factors are invisible to partners as well**, and the two are distinguished by whether the online-only extensions at step 1 were populated.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At step 7, more than half of students will find that the number of rows scored was smaller than the number requested, and fewer than a third will have noticed before the step required it.
predictions.instrument: step 7 reconciliations, with the artefact's revision history used to establish whether the discrepancy was recorded before or after the step was read. **If the discrepancy is rare, the day's point 10 is a documentation curiosity rather than an operational fact** and phase 6's agent case should be replaced.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: At step 5, more than half of students whose constructed class is absent from the taxonomy will report that cluster analysis did not recover it, and the modal missing attribute they name will be an access-path or device property rather than a content property.
predictions.instrument: step 5 clustering results and missing-attribute statements, coded by attribute type, cross-tabulated against the constructed class's defining dimension. **The modal attribute is the claim**: if students name content properties, they have not understood that the class is a class of person, and §8 objection 3's fix has not landed.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 1, more than a third of the log's incidents will be attributed by the cohort to a signal, and the log will show the actual detector was a person; the cohort will over-attribute to signals rather than under-attribute.
predictions.instrument: item 1 attributions against the log's recorded detector, coded for direction of error. **The direction is the claim.**

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 2, detection-latency estimates will be systematically low, and the underestimate will be largest for the partial-degradation incidents rather than the outages.
predictions.instrument: item 2 estimates against recorded times, split by incident class.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Fewer than one in five students will give a usable answer to item 3 before the day, and more than three-quarters will produce a liveness property at step 4 after it.
predictions.instrument: item 3 against step 4, paired per student. **If the before-figure is high, point 8 is not this day's content**; if the after-figure is low, the four-part target is not carrying liveness and needs a fifth part.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At step 6, more than a quarter of rota narrations will reveal that the recipient would not act on the signal as designed — and the proportion will be higher for signals whose false-alarm rate the student described as acceptable.
predictions.instrument: narrations coded for whether the recipient would act, cross-tabulated against the student's stated false-alarm rate. **The cross-tabulation tests whether the S038 countermeasure transferred**: if narrations are uniformly approving, the expert-politeness remedy did not survive the change of domain and step 6 is measuring courtesy again.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At step 5, more than a third of students will discover on their first attempt that stopping their signal produces no report at all, and the median gap between the demonstrated detection time and the step 8 committed latency will be large and in one direction — detection of the monitor's death slower than detection of the failure it watches for.
predictions.instrument: step 5 first-attempt outcomes and demonstrated times, paired against step 8 commitments. **The direction is the claim.** If the two are close, students are building liveness into the same path as the signal, which passes the step and fails point 4, and the specification needs a fifth part to the detection target rather than a separate step.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: At item 5, a large majority will predict that the agent's monitoring contains an error, and fewer than one in five will predict specifically that it will omit a liveness property.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded for generic error, wrong-threshold, and missing-liveness predictions, against what each agent produced. **This is the day's frontier measure and its second half is the one that matters**: a student who predicts a missing liveness property before the day has the day's content already, and if that rate is high the design's ordering is wrong.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At items 1 and 2, more than three-quarters of students will name a different party than the record shows decided, and the modal record answer will be *whoever was available* rather than either the evidence-holder or the authority-holder.
predictions.instrument: items 1 and 2 coded against the record, with the record's decider classified by role.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 3, a majority of students will discharge the escalation duty by telling one person, and the proportion will fall below a quarter when the same question is asked at the next morning's retrieval.
predictions.instrument: item 3 answers coded against point 4's three conditions, paired with the day-1 retrieval response. **If the next-morning figure does not move, point 4 is being learned as a list rather than as a standard.**

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At step 6, more than a third of not-detected entries across the cohort will be recorded as having no owner, and the unowned proportion will be highest for entries in the user-visible-only class.
predictions.instrument: step 6 assignments coded for owner presence and entry class. **If the unowned proportion is near zero, students are inventing owners** and the function-name fail condition is not catching it.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: More than a third of step 7 arrangements will be declined by the accountable staff member, and the modal ground will be the reversal path's cost rather than the owner or the authority.
predictions.instrument: step 7 outcomes and grounds, coded. **The modal ground is the claim**: the design predicts that students specify ownership carefully and reversal carelessly, because ownership is what the day is visibly about.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At phase 3's executed opening, more than three-quarters of groups will find at least one identity holding a gate-changing permission that no member of the group can name, and more than half will find that no member of the group can say who granted any assignment.
predictions.instrument: the groups' recorded answers against the actual assignment list. **If the unnameable-identity rate is low, the substrate's project has been provisioned more carefully than a real one** and the opening's finding will not transfer; the fallback is to run it against a second, older project.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: At step 8, the median number of arrangement parts a student records as enforced by nothing but agreement will be three or more, and the part most often recorded as unenforced will be the reversal path.
predictions.instrument: step 8 statements coded by part. **The modal unenforced part is the claim** and it is the same claim as prediction 4 from the other side: if students both specify reversal carelessly and leave it unenforced, the day's four parts are not equally weighted in practice and point 6 needs the emphasis point 2 currently has.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: More than a quarter of students will change their decision between item 1 and the artefact, and the modal direction will be from ship to conditional rather than from ship to no-ship.
predictions.instrument: item 1 against artefact item 1, coded for direction. **The modal direction is the claim**: a conditional is the move a student makes when re-reading their evidence has made them uncomfortable and the artefact still has to be written.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: More than half of artefact item 8 counter-arguments will be weaker than the same student's item 2, written before any evidence was re-read.
predictions.instrument: item 2 and item 8 paired and rated blind by the assessors against each other, not against a standard. **If this holds, the A4 mechanism does not survive being applied to oneself**, and [WP-069](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-069.md)'s proposed countermeasure is retracted for every contingent reuse under rule 5.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: The cohort's ship, no-ship and conditional split will not correlate with the strength of the students' evidence positions and will correlate with the quality of their detection designs.
predictions.instrument: decisions coded against independent ratings of artefact items 2 and 4. **If the split tracks the evidence instead, phase 6 point 2 is wrong** and the module has taught that a release decision is a quality decision after all.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: In the scoped S050 comparison, real-pressure conduct will diverge downward from constructed-pressure level for a majority of students.
predictions.instrument: the phase 5 part-two field, aggregated by direction. **This is the prediction the programme most needs to be wrong about**, because a systematic downward divergence means every level awarded on a constructed occasion in this programme is an overestimate — and §8 objection 1 states that the instrument is too weak to distinguish that finding from a dose effect, which is why the result is reported with its dose and not as a transfer estimate.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 9, fewer than half of students will state that their gate's judge has no published agreement with human judgement, despite the fact being taught at [S066](/wiki/seminars/S066.md) point 10, restated at that day's phase 8, and retrievable in one line.
predictions.instrument: item 9 second sentences, coded for whether the uncalibration is named. **If the rate is high, the module's most-repeated fact has landed and the fourth failure condition is redundant; if it is low, the design has evidence that a fact taught four times and never required in an artefact does not survive to the occasion that needs it** — which would be the strongest single result in this module and would bear directly on instrumentation rule 7.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: More than a quarter of item 9 third lists — what the student is relying on without having checked — will be empty, and empty third lists will be concentrated among students whose artefacts are longest.
predictions.instrument: item 9 third lists coded for emptiness, against artefact length and against the four-day intervention-record counts. **The correlation is the claim.** An empty third list on a four-day agent-assisted chain is not credible, and if it correlates with length rather than with intervention count then the artefact's polish is being produced by the tool and read as diligence — which is §8 objection 4 becoming measurable in the one place the design can currently see it.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Fewer than half of the exclusions each student sealed at [S055](/wiki/seminars/S055.md) will be re-labellable at item 1, and the modal stated reason for the remainder will be an intervention that is unavailable rather than an intervention that was run and gave a mixed result.
predictions.instrument: item 1 responses coded label-now / cannot-label, with cannot-label reasons coded by whether the named intervention is available on the substrate. **If the modal reason is a mixed result instead, S055's exclusion route was being used to avoid a judgement rather than to record an inconclusive one**, and S055's humility measure means something different from what that day claimed.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: More than half of all step 4 boundary lines will carry a blank enforcement field on first submission, and the distribution will be bimodal — a small number of students with almost none, and most with almost all.
predictions.instrument: step 4 lines coded for enforcement presence, per student, before and after the [S073](/wiki/seminars/S073.md) step 5 revision. **If blanks are rare, either the boundaries are trivial or students are naming enforcement that does not exist**; the two are distinguished at S073 step 5, where the enforcement must be located on the student's own control-flow drawing.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: The rota member's decline-week estimates will be systematically earlier than the peers' for the same stated rates.
predictions.instrument: phase 7's two distributions compared by median week per student. **If the peers are earlier or the two agree, the rule 1 correction bought nothing on this day**, and §8 objection 2's fix is correct in principle and empty in practice — which would be a finding about rule 1's reach rather than about this day.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: A majority of step 6 predictions will name no action that appears in the step 7 shadow run, and the modal missed action will be one whose reversal is social rather than technical.
predictions.instrument: step 6 and step 7 pairs coded for match; misses coded by reversibility class. **This is the prediction the module most needs to be wrong about**, because [S074](/wiki/seminars/S074.md) step 3 is built to consume the unanticipated set and a small set makes that element thin. If the misses concentrate on socially-irreversible actions, point 7's scope statement is the day's most load-bearing sentence and is currently carried by one artefact clause.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 5, a large majority will predict that the agent grants more than asked, and a small minority will predict *where* — that the prohibition is expressed in the agent's instructions rather than in a schema, a permission, a precondition or a rate.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded generic / specific, against what each student's agent actually produced at step 2, with the location of the produced prohibition coded into the same six categories used at [S073](/wiki/seminars/S073.md) phase 8. **The gap between the two rates is this day's frontier-calibration measure**, and the design's expectation is that it is wide. **If the specific rate is high, the cohort already holds point 5 and the day's central instruction is redundant**, which would be the most surprising result in the module and would mean two years of agent practice taught something the design assumed it did not.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: The intervention records' acceptance counts will be **absent or implausibly round** for a substantial minority of artefacts on first submission.
predictions.instrument: step 5 acceptance counts coded present / absent / round-number, joined to the correction count. **A missing denominator is the finding**, not a paperwork failure: it is direct evidence for §8 objection 3's claim that a student who is not reading the output is also not counting it, and it is the datum that decides whether the field should be proposed to the [Copilot Practice Standard](/wiki/program/12-Copilot-Practice-Standard.md) or withdrawn. **Instrumentation note, for the compliance register.** The entry this paper's §8 objection 2 requires, stated so that it can be transcribed without re-derivation: *[WP-071](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-071.md) §8 — [S071](/wiki/seminars/S071.md) phase 7 measured with a peer a judgement an available external observer was positioned to make, and did not carry [S068](/wiki/seminars/S068.md) step 5's remedy across. Rule: instrumentation rules 1 and 5. Status: **Fixed**. Reason: violation of two written rules, with the remedy already in the design's repertoire; no design judgement was in contest.* **A second note, for the [Copilot Practice Standard](/wiki/program/12-Copilot-Practice-Standard.md), argued and not enacted.** §8 objection 3's fix, stated so it can be transcribed if this day's outcome supports it: **"The intervention record states the number of agent outputs accepted without change alongside the corrections. A record of corrections without a count of acceptances is a numerator without a denominator, and the decline-rate test [S071](/wiki/seminars/S071.md) point 8 establishes cannot be computed from it."** Provenance: proposed at [WP-071](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-071.md) §8, used at [S071](/wiki/seminars/S071.md) only, contingent under instrumentation rule 5 as amended, and tested by §9 prediction 6. **This paper cannot edit a shared page and does not.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 4, more than half of the cohort will write a number for a system whose loop makes its path set unbounded, and the numbers written will cluster near the count of drawn branches rather than near the cap.
predictions.instrument: item 4 responses coded number / unbounded, with numeric answers compared against both the drawn-branch count and the cap. **The clustering is the claim**: if the numbers cluster near the cap instead, students are treating the loop as a construct and mis-computing it, which is a different and much smaller problem.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: No group will predict the phase 3 reversal, and after it, more than half of step 4 task characterisations will name a mix change that would invalidate their own pattern choice.
predictions.instrument: group rankings on task 2 recorded before the records are supplied; step 4 characterisations coded for whether the named invalidating change is one their pattern would actually fail on. **If groups predict the reversal, the first task's construction is not defeating expectation and P1's win is being read as a demonstration rather than as a finding.**

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: The number of realised paths touching an [S071](/wiki/seminars/S071.md)-prohibited action will be greater than zero for a majority of students, and the breaches will concentrate on prohibitions whose enforcement field was blank.
predictions.instrument: step 7 breach counts joined to the [S071](/wiki/seminars/S071.md) step 4 enforcement records. **If breaches concentrate on prohibitions that had a named enforcement, the enforcement points students named do not exist**, which is a finding about [S071](/wiki/seminars/S071.md)'s step 4 rather than about this day and would be the strongest available evidence for [WP-071](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-071.md) §5's fluency failure.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Step 6's *one path not on your drawing* will be answered correctly by fewer students than step 6's *least frequent path*, and the gap will be large.
predictions.instrument: step 6 and step 7 pairs coded separately for the two clauses. **The gap is the claim**: predicting the frequency of a path you drew is interpolation, and predicting a path you did not draw requires knowing what your own representation omits, which is the competence [S073](/wiki/seminars/S073.md) needs and which this design believes the cohort does not yet have.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At step 1's added clause, more than half of first submissions will name a composition that **is** one of the framework's five under a different description, and the modal error will be a fan-out with a model-selected aggregator offered as unnamed.
predictions.instrument: step 1 compositions coded against the framework's catalogue at delivery. **This is §8 objection 3's test and it is written to lose the design's bet**: if students cannot produce a composition outside the catalogue, the mapping has replaced the constructs rather than illustrating them, and point 9 should be moved out of phase 4 into a handout that is not taught.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: At item 5, the modal sealed prediction will be that the agent produces a *correct drawing with a wrong bound*, and the agent's stated bound will cluster with the room's at item 4 rather than with the cap.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded against the agent's actual output per student, with agent bounds compared to drawn-branch counts and to the cap on the same axis as item 4. **The clustering is the claim.** If the agent bounds correctly while the room does not, the day has an unusually clean frontier datum in the opposite direction from the one the design expects, and the phase 6 agent case is the wrong case. **Instrumentation note, for the compliance register.** The entry §8 objection 1 requires, stated so that it can be transcribed without re-derivation: *[WP-072](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-072.md) §8 — [S072](/wiki/seminars/S072.md) phase 3 generalised from a single task record and did not carry [S017](/wiki/seminars/S017.md) phase 3's second-workload remedy across. Rule: instrumentation rule 5. Status: **Fixed**. Reason: violation of a written rule with the remedy already in the repertoire and cited in the same day's phase 2; no design judgement was in contest.* The paper additionally argues, without enacting, for **a rule-5 checklist maintained alongside the compliance register**, listing each remedy in the repertoire with the failure it addresses, to be consulted at §5 of every whitepaper — on the ground that rule 5 is the only instrumentation rule with no checkable trigger and has now failed twice in two consecutive days.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 1, the cohort will name more omissions in the *specification promises what the tool does not do* direction than in the *tool does what the specification does not mention* direction, and the asymmetry will be larger than it was at [S034](/wiki/seminars/S034.md).
predictions.instrument: item 1 responses coded by direction and compared per student against the [S034](/wiki/seminars/S034.md) item 4 result. **The widening asymmetry is the claim**: an over-promising specification is found by reading, and an under-describing one is found only by using the tool, which is the habit this module needs and which four quarters of contract work have not built.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 4, the median predicted crossing count will be lower than the substrate's inventory by more than a factor of two, and the systematically missed category will be values the system itself authored under an earlier request and read back.
predictions.instrument: item 4 responses against the inventory, with misses coded by the author category at point 4. **If the missed category is third-party document content instead, the room is already thinking about external content and the day's problem is narrower than §1 claims.**

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At step 5, more entries will be closed by accepted re-declaration than by enforcement point, and the ratio will be higher for [S071](/wiki/seminars/S071.md) prohibitions than for [S072](/wiki/seminars/S072.md) breach paths.
predictions.instrument: step 5 closures coded three ways and split by source list. **The differential is the claim**: a breach the student watched happen is harder to accept than a prohibition they wrote in the abstract, and if the two rates are equal then observing a breach changes nothing about how it is treated, which would be a finding about [S072](/wiki/seminars/S072.md)'s step 7 rather than about this day.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: More than a quarter of step 4 reductions will cost nothing — the student will narrow the schema without giving up any request a substrate user makes.
predictions.instrument: step 4 cost statements checked against the substrate's request log at phase 7. **If this holds it is not a failure of the students**; it means the substrate's tool schemas are broader than its usage requires by a wide margin, which is a finding about the substrate that [S076](/wiki/seminars/S076.md) will consume, and the design predicts it will be the single most actionable result the day produces for the platform.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At step 7's attempted prohibited call, **more than a third of attempts will succeed**, and among those refused, more than a quarter will be refused by a mechanism other than the one the student named at step 5.
predictions.instrument: attempted calls coded refused / succeeded, with the refusing mechanism recorded and joined to the step 5 entry for the same prohibition. **Both halves are the claim.** A high success rate is direct evidence for §8 objection 3 and for [WP-071](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-071.md) §8 objection 1, and it is the first such evidence the programme has. **A high wrong-mechanism rate is the more interesting result**: it would mean students are protected by enforcement they did not identify, which is point 2's second named omission — enforcement downstream of the boundary — measured rather than asserted, and it would make the case for widening step 5 to require a downstream inventory.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: At item 5, the modal predicted location for the agent's prohibition will be the tool's description, and the modal actual location will be the same.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses and produced artefacts both coded into the six locations reported at phase 8. **Agreement is the claim, and agreement is the uncomfortable result**: it would mean the cohort can predict the failure and would not have caught it, because predicting where an artefact will be wrong and reviewing for it are different acts. If the room predicts the description and the agent uses a schema constraint, the instrument has found a capability the design did not credit and the phase 6 agent case needs replacing. **Instrumentation note.** No compliance-register entry is required by this paper. §8 objection 2's finding is a **recorded** widening argument rather than a violation of a written rule, since the rule as written does not reach backward reliance; the day's fix was taken anyway, on rule 5 grounds, and is annotated at the point of change. **§8 objection 3's fix is likewise annotated in the day and requires no register entry**: it repairs an internal inconsistency between the day's own teaching and its own assessment rather than a violation of a shared rule, and the argument for it is carried here so that it can be disagreed with.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 2, the cohort's outcome enumeration will include the fourth outcome — returned something plausible and wrong — for fewer than half of students, and the count will not be higher than the same cohort's [S033](/wiki/seminars/S033.md) item 1 count for the first three.
predictions.instrument: item 2 responses coded against the four outcomes and joined per student to the [S033](/wiki/seminars/S033.md) baseline. **The second clause is the claim**: if the first three outcomes are enumerated better than at S033, four quarters of intervening material improved a retained enumeration, which this design does not expect and would be the most interesting retention result in the module.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 3, more than half of the observation-position claims will name a party, and at step 4 the same students will write *none* for selection and output utilisation. The shift will be large.
predictions.instrument: item 3 and step 4 claims paired per student and coded party / none, by shape. **If the shift is small because item 3 already answers *none*, the day's problem is smaller than §1 claims** and the bridge is doing less work than the design credits it with.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At step 2, the shape students most often report being unable to find in the trace log will be output utilisation, and the second will be selection.
predictions.instrument: step 2 shape-not-found responses tallied by shape. **This is the prediction the design is most confident of and it is the one worth being wrong about**: if students find output-utilisation instances readily, the log contains more evidence than point 2 predicts it can, which would mean the substrate has instrumentation the design has not accounted for and the criterion's boundary is drawn in the wrong place.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: More than half of step 5 discriminations will fail the independence requirement on first submission, and the modal failure will be a discrimination that compares the trace against itself.
predictions.instrument: step 5 submissions coded against the fail condition, before and after revision. **If independence failures are rare, [S068](/wiki/seminars/S068.md) point 4 has transferred**, which would be the strongest available evidence that a remedy taught five weeks earlier survives a change of object — and this design's expectation is that it will not, because the record here looks like an external artefact in a way a monitoring pipeline does not.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At step 4's added clause, more than a third of first submissions will describe what a same-named evaluator **computes** rather than what it **reads**, and a smaller but non-trivial number will name an evaluator as the observing party despite the specification's fail condition.
predictions.instrument: step 4 responses coded reads / computes / evaluator-as-party, by shape. **The computes-rather-than-reads answer is the finding**, not the outright violation: it is the form in which a student holds the taxonomy and has not held the criterion, and it is exactly what §8 objection 3 predicts the platform's availability produces. **If the clause is answered correctly at a high rate on first submission, the objection is weaker than this paper argues** and point 9 is doing more work than it is credited with.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: At item 5, the shape the cohort nominates as their agent's worst will be execution or input, and the shapes appearing most often in their own [S071](/wiki/seminars/S071.md) to [S073](/wiki/seminars/S073.md) frontier statements will be selection or output utilisation.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded by shape, joined to a blind coding of the three prior frontier statements per student. **The disagreement is the claim, and it is the module's recursion made measurable**: it would show the cohort nominating the shapes their tools report and living with the shapes nothing reports, which is point 2 recovered from two years of their own practice. If the two agree, the cohort's model of its own instrument is better than the design assumes. **Instrumentation note, for the shared pages.** Two changes this paper argues for and cannot make. *For the [Durable and Perishable Register](/wiki/program/09-Durable-and-Perishable-Register.md).* The durable entry currently reads *The four shapes of tool failure | S074 | A decomposition, not an implementation.* It should read: **"The four shapes of tool failure, decomposed by observational position rather than by stage | S074 | A claim about who is positioned to observe, independent of any implementation. The count of silent shapes is not part of the durable claim — see [WP-074](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-074.md) §8."** **The corresponding qualifications on [M15](/wiki/modules/M15.md) and [Q8](/wiki/quarters/Q8.md) are already made**; this entry is the remainder. *For the [Seminar Day Design Pattern](/wiki/program/04-Seminar-Day-Design-Pattern.md).* The elevation §8 objection 2 argues for, stated so it can be transcribed: **"An instrument administered after its answer has been taught measures recall. Where a day's instrument is administered inside or after phase 4, the day must either administer it before phase 4 as well and report the movement, or state in its whitepaper that the instrument measures retention rather than reasoning."** Provenance: opened at [WP-054](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-054.md) §8 at one instance with the rule form already stated; second instance at [WP-062](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-062.md) §8 and [WP-066](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-066.md) §8; third at [WP-074](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-074.md) §8, found only because the prior two had recorded it. **No number is assigned here.** Instrumentation rule 7 is already pending on a separate observation and this paper does not renumber anything.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: The room will produce the routing-record argument at phase 2's bridge in under three minutes, **and a majority of groups will still rank E3 first at phase 3** before the records arrive.
predictions.instrument: phase 2 bridge timing and answer quality recorded; phase 3 group rankings recorded before records are supplied. **The conjunction is the claim.** If both hold, the closure [WP-052](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-052.md) §6 asked for has been made and the transfer has not, which is the state §7 reports as honest. **If the room ranks E4 first, the transfer fires and WP-052 §6's pessimism about this retrieval was wrong** — which would be the most encouraging result in the module.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 2, fewer than half of students will change their judgement of the run when the tool results are removed.
predictions.instrument: item 1 and item 2 judgements paired per student, reported with the demand characteristic per §8 objection 2. **The direction is the claim and the magnitude is not asserted**, because the instrument is compromised in the direction of over-reporting movement; a result above half is uninterpretable and a result below half is informative, which is an asymmetric instrument and is stated as one.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: More than a quarter of students who run an intervention at step 5 will find a step their evaluation scored well on whose removal did not change the outcome.
predictions.instrument: step 5 results coded for outcome movement, per student, with the intervention type recorded. **This is the closure's real evidence and the prediction the design most wants on record**, because it is a measurement of the students' own systems rather than of their reading. **If the rate is near zero, either the substrate's capabilities are unusually tight or students are choosing safe interventions**, and the two are distinguished by the intervention-type distribution.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: The phase 7 inversion-construction success rate will be **lower** than the same cohort's [S048](/wiki/seminars/S048.md) rate.
predictions.instrument: phase 7 first-obligation outcomes recorded and joined per student to the [S048](/wiki/seminars/S048.md) baseline. **The direction is the claim and it is [WP-048](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-048.md) §6's own prediction tested**: constructing a pair of runs an evaluation ranks wrongly requires holding the unit, the judge and the trajectory's ordering simultaneously, which is strictly harder than constructing an output pair. **If the rate is equal or higher, WP-048 §6 was wrong that its method does not extend**, and point 6's break at the reorder test is narrower than the day claims.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At step 2, **the modal agent-proposed unit will be the episode**, and more than half of students will choose a different one.
predictions.instrument: step 2's agent-proposed-unit record and the student's chosen unit, tabulated jointly. **The conjunction is the claim and it is §8 objection 3's test.** If the agent proposes the episode and students mostly depart from it, the day's instruction has survived the instrument's default and the recursion is being managed rather than merely named. **If students mostly accept the proposal, the day has taught the lesson and supplied the tool that undoes it**, and the disagreement build §8 declined has to be found room for by cutting something else from phase 5.

predictions.label: Prediction 6.
predictions.claim: At item 5, fewer than one student in five will predict that the agent's evaluation will be correct and will answer a different question; the modal prediction will be a defect in the code or the configuration.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded defect / wrong-question / other, against what each student's agent produced. **The low wrong-question rate is the claim**, and it is the module's closing frontier finding: five days of predicting agent failure will have taught the cohort to expect errors and not to expect correct answers to unasked questions, which is the harder and more consequential prediction and the one the design has not managed to teach anywhere. **Instrumentation note.** No compliance-register entry is required by this paper. All three §8 findings are design judgements between defensible options — a sequencing choice, an instrument choice and a phase-budget choice — and are **recorded** rather than fixed under the register's criterion, with the two cheap repairs taken and the two expensive ones named and declined. The one shared-page change this paper depends on is [WP-074](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-074.md) §9's, which supplies the wording for the elevation this day applies voluntarily and contingently.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At phase 1, students will mark under half of the externally influenceable portion of the printed context, and the systematic omissions will be the tool outputs and the orchestration summary rather than the retrieved documents.
predictions.instrument: item 1 markings scored against the context's true influence map, reported **by source class rather than in aggregate**. The class breakdown is the claim; an aggregate under-marking rate would be consistent with several accounts, and only the class pattern distinguishes the perimeter model from ordinary incompleteness.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: More than two thirds of item 3's enforcement answers will fall in point 6's first place — restricting what reaches the assembler.
predictions.instrument: item 3 free-text answers coded into the three places by two raters blind to each other. **If the answers are already distributed across the three, the perimeter model is not the entry state the day is built on**, and phase 3's ordering is solving a problem the cohort does not have.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Groups will rank C1 highest and C4 lowest before the behaviour is shown, and C4's provenance reconstruction error will be the highest of the four.
predictions.instrument: committed rankings against the agent's measured behaviour, and task 1's per-case error rate. **If C4 is ranked accurately, the payload has failed** and the reserve case in §5 is the fallback rather than the design.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At step 7, more students will produce an addition described as a removal than will produce a removal, and the discriminating question — who now cannot do this — will be unanswerable for the majority of first attempts.
predictions.instrument: step 7 entries coded for whether a person or role lost a capability, with the rota member's phase 5 challenge recorded. **If most students produce genuine removals unprompted, point 7 is not the difficulty this design treats it as**, and phase 5's fading should move to step 7 instead of step 6.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 5, a large majority will predict that the agent's injection hardening will be wrong, and a small minority will name that it will add a filter and leave the tool schema untouched.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded for generic-versus-specific failure identification, against what each student's agent actually produced, and against the point 6 place its output falls in. **The gap between the two rates is the day's frontier measure.** If the specific rate is high, the room's model of the agent is better than the design assumes and the phase 6 agent case is redundant; **if the room's own item 3 answers and the agent's outputs land in the same place in the same proportions, the day has a finding it did not design for** — that the tool's failure mode and the room's are the same failure mode — and it should be reported as the module's most useful result rather than as a coincidence.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Fewer than one student in ten will object to phase 1 item 1's premise that each incident had an adversary.
predictions.instrument: item 1 responses coded for any challenge to the framing, including hedged ones. **This is the prediction the design most expects to be right and least wants to be**, and a high objection rate would mean the cohort arrives with the discrimination the module is built to install, which would make phase 3's payload redundant and would be reported as such.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 3, students will report that their [S068](/wiki/seminars/S068.md) detection design would have caught T1 and T2 at a rate substantially above the true rate, and their T3 answers will be roughly accurate.
predictions.instrument: item 3 answers per record against the components' actual signal coverage, **reported per attack rather than in aggregate**. The per-attack split is the claim; an overall optimism figure is consistent with general overconfidence and would not establish that the invisibility is specific to the function and the answer channel.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: More than half of step 2's cost figures will carry *estimated from no data* or an equivalent, and at phase 7 more partners will attack the control than will interrogate the cost estimate.
predictions.instrument: provenance values coded, and phase 7 outcomes coded for which of the two the partner engaged. **The second half is the test of objection 2**: if students treat their own unsourced figures as settled once the field is filled in, the day has trained the form and not the scepticism, and the ordinal-ranking fix should be reconsidered.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Step 5's exhaustion arithmetic will reach budget before capacity or quota for a clear majority of components, and the students whose commitment shape was chosen at [S064](/wiki/seminars/S064.md) against a demand forecast will be over-represented in that majority.
predictions.instrument: step 5 results coded by which constraint is reached first, joined to each student's [S064](/wiki/seminars/S064.md) commitment shape. **If the constraint reached first is unrelated to the commitment shape, point 4's central claim — that the attack lands on whichever commitment is weakest, and that this is a property of your commitments rather than your architecture — is wrong**, and the day is teaching a dependency that does not hold.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At phase 3's T1 execution, the evaluation-score movement will be indistinguishable from zero for every group, and at step 3 the proportion of recording-gap entries resting on an unpublished-accuracy control will exceed the proportion resting on a signal the student's own component emits.
predictions.instrument: the T1 score deltas per group, and step 3 entries coded for whether the named distinguisher is the student's own instrumentation or a platform detection. **The second half is the test of whether point 9 landed.** If students overwhelmingly cite platform detections as their distinguishers, the day has taught them where the products are rather than what their own systems record, which is the opposite of step 3's purpose and would require point 9 to move after step 3 rather than before it.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 4, a majority of students will predict that adding the check degrades all principals roughly equally, and the measured effect at step 3 will be concentrated on the most restricted class.
predictions.instrument: item 4 free-text predictions coded for whether they identify a class at all, joined to the step 3 measurement's shape. **The claim is about the coding of the prediction, not its magnitude**: a student who predicts a uniform effect has a different model from one who predicts the wrong class, and only the first is the schema failure §1 describes.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 3, more than half of students will answer with a mechanism rather than a duration, and their durations, where given, will be shorter than the measured staleness latency at step 5.
predictions.instrument: item 3 answers coded as duration or mechanism, and the durations compared signed against step 5. **If the durations are accurate, staleness is already held as a latency** and point 5 is a formalisation rather than an introduction, which would move it out of phase 4 and into the artefact form.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Groups will rank P4 as leaking least before the records are supplied, and will rank P3 as leaking least *after* them.
predictions.instrument: committed rankings against post-record rankings, per placement. **The second half is the interesting one**: P3 silently truncates, which is a leak of a different kind, and a room that moves from P4 to P3 has learned that a control can be correct and irrelevant without yet learning that absence is informative — which is what phase 6 is for and would be evidence that the clinic is doing work.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: For at least a quarter of the cohort, the least-privileged principal class at step 3 will contain fewer than ten principals.
predictions.instrument: step 3 class sizes, which specification rule 2 requires in the same field as the result. **This is the direct test of §8 objection 2**, and if it holds for more than half the cohort, the per-class measurement is not a measurement on this substrate and the design must either change the substrate's permission structure or stop claiming the finding is the student's own.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 5, a large majority of agents will produce the string-filter approach; fewer than one student in five will have predicted that specifically; and **fewer than one in ten will have predicted the missing chunk projection.** At step 6, a majority of pipelines that chunk will be found not to project permissions.
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded against what each agent produced, and step 6 results in three categories. **The step 6 rate is the claim that matters.** If most pipelines already project correctly, the chunking run is a demonstration of a solved problem for this cohort and its phase 3 slot should go to the reserve placement in §5; if the rate is high, the day has found a live defect in the cohort's own production retrieval paths, and that finding belongs to the substrate's data owner within the week rather than to a phase 8 slide.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 2, students will over-report that their [S070](/wiki/seminars/S070.md) commitment fired, and the largest single category at step 1 will be *condition occurred and nothing fired*.
predictions.instrument: item 2 against the alert history, and step 1's four categories. **The second half is the claim.** If the largest category is *condition did not occur*, the quarter was quiet and §8 objection 1's failure case has occurred, which the design must report as such rather than as a result about detection.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: Item 3's signed latency errors will run in one direction: students will predict detection faster than they committed, and both will be faster than realised.
predictions.instrument: the three-way comparison reported signed, per student. **The sign is the claim, not the magnitude**, and a symmetric distribution would mean latency estimation is noisy rather than optimistic — which is a different defect with a different remedy and would move the response from point 8 to step 2's reference discipline.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At item 1, more than two thirds of students will give a confident start date for at least one of the series that has no start.
predictions.instrument: item 1 dates coded against which series have an identifiable onset. **If most students decline to give a date for the drift series, point 1 is not the difficulty this design treats it as** and the phase 2 bridge is answering a question the room does not have.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At step 7, a majority of rota members will name a mute condition that the student's own design makes likely — a false-alarm rate the design permits, or an action the recipient cannot take from home.
predictions.instrument: mute answers coded against the student's own stated false-alarm rate and the contract's third part. **If mute conditions are unrelated to the design, the mute question is measuring the rota's disposition rather than the artefact**, the proposed remedy is retracted under rule 5, and the [S087](/wiki/seminars/S087.md) commitment built on it is withdrawn.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 6, a large majority will predict the agent's monitoring configuration will be wrong and fewer than a fifth will name the absent liveness property; and at step 4, a majority of first-draft designs will carry liveness on inherited signals and not on the detector built that morning.
predictions.instrument: item 6 responses coded for generic-versus-specific failure identification, and step 4 entries coded by which signals carry liveness before the phase 7 challenge. **The two rates should move together and the claim is that they will.** If students name the agent's omission and then commit it themselves, the day has taught a fact about a tool and not a property of monitoring design, and point 4 should be delivered against the cohort's own step 4 drafts rather than against A4.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: Fewer than a third of students will write *undecided* at item 3, and the students who do will have a higher mean level than those who decided, because the discriminating-evidence requirement is harder to satisfy for a decided position than for an undecided one.
predictions.instrument: item 3 positions coded, joined to awarded levels. **The second half is the claim.** If undecided positions cluster at the bottom, the failure condition is being read as a safe option rather than as a demanding one, and the specification's wording has produced the opposite of its intent.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: More than half of first-draft mechanisms will contain at least one unrewritten "X did Y", and the on-call member's phase 4 question will surface a further one in a majority of the remainder.
predictions.instrument: accounts coded for person-as-actor constructions before the defence, and the defence transcripts coded for constructions surfaced there. **The gap between the two counts is the measure of how mechanical the rewriting was**, and a small gap means students are applying the rule and not the reason.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: The cohort's [S077](/wiki/seminars/S077.md)-to-today attribution transition will run toward *undecided* rather than toward the opposite classification.
predictions.instrument: the phase 5 part two transition table. **If students who misclassified an accident as an attack three weeks ago now classify confidently in the other direction, the module has taught a correction rather than a discrimination**, which is a worse outcome than the original error and would require [S077](/wiki/seminars/S077.md)'s T4 to be rebuilt as something other than a reversal.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At [S089](/wiki/seminars/S089.md), the largest category for this day's recommendations will be *never answered* rather than implemented or declined.
predictions.instrument: the [S089](/wiki/seminars/S089.md) disposition element, coded three ways. **This is a prediction about the organisation and not about the students**, and if it holds it is the most important finding either day produces: a handover whose recommendations are neither taken nor refused is the ordinary fate of a post-incident report, and no part of this programme currently teaches what to do about it.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: A majority of students will use an agent for at least the timeline, and **the number of unverified agent-supplied entries surfaced at phase 4 will exceed the number recorded by students in their own intervention records.**
predictions.instrument: intervention records coded for corrections to agent-supplied timeline entries, against the defence transcripts coded for entries the assessors surfaced. **The gap is the measure of whether the sourcing discipline was applied or performed.** If the two counts are close, the module's four preceding intervention records have installed the habit and the day should say so; if the defence surfaces substantially more, the discipline is being written rather than run, and item 1's marking rule needs an artefact-side check that the day does not currently have.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 1, more than three-quarters of students will list no people at all, and at step 3 nearly all will name three.
predictions.instrument: item 1 component lists coded for person-entries, paired with step 3. **The pairing is the claim, not the item 1 figure**: a high item 1 rate would mean the cohort already holds the day's premise and phase 3 is over-built, and a low step 3 rate would mean the frame is not usable on a real service.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At the phase 3 task-after, groups will produce *absorbing* and *routing* unprompted and will not produce *licensing*.
predictions.instrument: task-after categories coded against the trichotomy, by group. **This is the prediction the day's branch depends on**, and if licensing is produced freely while routing is not, [S084](/wiki/seminars/S084.md)'s case selection inverts and the design's account of which dependency is hardest to see is wrong.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: More than half of students will mark do-not-know at step 5's moved-work question, and among those who do not, the majority of identified instances will be inside the students' own service rather than in a receiving team.
predictions.instrument: step 5 entries coded for do-not-know and, where present, for the location of the moved work relative to the student's boundary. **The second half is the informative one**: work that moves inside your own boundary is work you can see, and finding only those means the frame has been applied and O4's actual mechanism has not been.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At phase 5, the two maintainers will materially correct more than a third of the descriptions given to them, and the corrections will concentrate on students whose step 3 provenance is recorded as *org chart* rather than *observed* or *asked*.
predictions.instrument: maintainer corrections recorded and coded against the provenance field. **If corrections are distributed evenly across provenance**, the provenance field is not measuring anything and the checked element should be removed rather than kept as a formality.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 5, a large majority will predict that the agent produces a good inventory, and **fewer than a quarter will name that a resource inventory has no field for a person.**
predictions.instrument: item 5 responses coded on two axes — whether the quality prediction was made, and whether the structural absence was named — reported as two rates rather than one. **The gap between the rates is the day's frontier-calibration measure and the two-axis coding is the claim.** A cohort that predicts the agent will do well has predicted nothing, because they have used it for five quarters; a cohort that names what it cannot be about has located a boundary. **If the second rate is high, this module's frontier argument is already held and phase 3's executed opening is redundant. If both rates are low, the cohort is not yet forming predictions about the agent at all**, which is a finding about the whole [Copilot Practice Standard](/wiki/program/12-Copilot-Practice-Standard.md) and not about this day.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 2, the set of parties who can stop the deployment and the set who cannot complain about it will be near-disjoint for a large majority of students, and a majority of item 1 lists will contain nobody in the second set at all.
predictions.instrument: item 2 responses coded for set membership and overlap. **The second clause is the claim**: a disjoint pair of non-empty sets means the cohort can see both and has not connected them, and an empty second set means they cannot see one, which are different findings requiring different days.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At phase 3, groups will rank M3 above M4 before the outcome is supplied, and the reason given will refer to coverage rather than to method.
predictions.instrument: rankings with free-text justification, coded for whether the justification names a property of the method. **If groups rank M4 first for the right reason, the phase is over-built** and the day should open at the task-after.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At step 6, more than a third of findings will be accepted by the decision-owner, and the modal ground for declining will be information the student did not have rather than disagreement about the finding.
predictions.instrument: step 6 outcomes and grounds, recorded by the staff member and coded. **The modal ground is the claim, and it is the prediction the day most needs to hold**, because a cohort whose findings are declined on the merits has learned something different from a cohort whose findings are declined because they were wrong about the facts — and only the second is a lesson about their own analysis.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At phase 7, fewer than half of hypothesised unstated interests will survive the partner's good-faith account.
predictions.instrument: phase 7 outcomes coded for survival, with the distinguishing evidence recorded where the hypothesis survived. **If nearly all survive, the phase is not working as a countermeasure** and the cohort is constructing accounts designed to lose, which is the same defect [WP-070](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-070.md) §9 prediction 2 anticipates in the mechanism this structure reuses — and a failure there retracts this reuse under instrumentation rule 5.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 5, a large majority will predict that M5 is longer than their own item 1 list, and **fewer than a third will name possession of an identity as its frame.** Separately, **more than a quarter of step 3 entries will treat a zero-result query as evidence that a party has no material, despite a correctly written frame sentence at step 8.**
predictions.instrument: item 5 coded on two axes; step 3 entries coded for whether the inference drawn exceeds the frame the same student wrote, cross-tabulated against the frame sentence's correctness. **The cross-tabulation is the claim and it is §8 objection 3's test.** If frame-correct students draw corpus-to-world inferences at the same rate as frame-incorrect ones, the checked element is a formality and the build is teaching what the objection says it teaches. **If the rate is near zero, the objection is answered and the paper was wrong to concede it.**

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 2, fewer than a third of students will be able to name both the decision their risk bears on and its date.
predictions.instrument: item 2 responses coded for a named decision and a named date, separately. **The separation is the claim**: naming a decision without a date is a different and lesser failure than naming neither, and only the second means the student is writing into a vacuum.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At phase 3, groups will rank R2 above R3 and will rank both below R1, and the modal reason given for R1 will be its completeness.
predictions.instrument: rankings with free-text justification, coded for whether the justification names completeness, decidability or outcome. **If R1 is ranked below R3, the cohort already prefers a recommendation to a qualified statement** and the day's problem is R3's rather than R1's, which changes what phase 4 needs to weight.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: More than a quarter of decisions at step 6 will go against the student's recommendation, and item 4's predictions will under-estimate that rate.
predictions.instrument: step 6 outcomes against item 4 predictions, paired. **This prediction is contaminated by the briefing effect §8 objection 2 describes and is reported with that contamination attached**; the interpretable half is the item 4 gap, which is a claim about students' expectations rather than about decision-makers' behaviour.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At phase 7, more than half of partners will be unable to name a decision the statement drove, and the failure will concentrate on statements whose step 3 interval was carried over in parameter units.
predictions.instrument: phase 7 outcomes coded for whether a decision was named, cross-tabulated against the step 3 interval's unit. **The cross-tabulation is the claim**: if decidability failures are evenly distributed across interval units, the unit conversion is not the mechanism the day says it is, and point 5 is a stylistic preference rather than a functional requirement.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: Groups will rank R5 above R4 before the outcomes are supplied, at a rate above half; **and students who completed the step 8 build will deliver statements no more decidable, at phase 7, than students who delivered without the figure.**
predictions.instrument: R5 rankings with justification; and phase 7 decision-naming rates cross-tabulated against whether the student's figure was ready at step 6. **The second half is §8 objection 3's test and the design expects to lose it in one of two directions.** If build-completers are *less* decidable, the build is resourcing the failure and should be moved out of the day. If they are *more* decidable, the objection is answered and the paper conceded too readily. **A null result is the least useful outcome and is the most likely**, because the sample is one cohort and the effect, if any, is small — which is itself worth stating in advance, per [S028](/wiki/seminars/S028.md)'s own discipline applied to this design.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 1, more than half of students will give an estimate wrong by a factor of two or more against the measured rate, and the errors will be predominantly over-estimates.
predictions.instrument: item 1 estimates against measured usage, coded for direction and magnitude band. **The direction is the claim**: symmetric error would mean the cohort is guessing, and systematic over-estimation means they are reasoning from having shipped it, which is a different finding and the one the day assumes.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 3, training or communication will appear first on more than three-quarters of intervention lists, and fewer than a fifth will name anything from point 7's four controllable levers.
predictions.instrument: item 3 responses coded by intervention class and by position in the list. **If the levers appear freely, point 4 is not the correction the day thinks it is** and phase 4 should reweight toward point 8.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At step 2, the workaround-purpose do-not-know rate will exceed half, and among students whose named user attends at step 6, more than a third of those do-not-knows will be resolved in that thirty minutes.
predictions.instrument: step 2 marks paired with step 6 records, coded for resolution. **The second half is the claim and it is the day's argument in one number**: if asking resolves the question this readily, the reason nobody knows what workarounds are for is that nobody asks.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At phase 7, more than a third of step 6 records will contain at least one inference recorded as an observation, and the rate will be lower than the same cohort's [S037](/wiki/seminars/S037.md) rate two years earlier.
predictions.instrument: phase 7 outcomes against the students' own S037 column ratios. **This is the test of [WP-037](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-037.md) §6's forward claim.** If the rate has not fallen, a student who has watched someone work does **not** have a durable category for the said/done/inferred distinction, the claim that day made about this one is wrong, and the discipline needs re-teaching rather than retrieving.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 5, a large majority will predict that the agent returns a number, and **fewer than a third will name that the number is about requests rather than people. Independently, more than a third of step 8 dimensions will resolve to a single value on first deployment**, committing the error phase 6's agent case demonstrates.
