predictions.instrument: item 5 coded on two axes; step 8 dimension cardinality recorded on first deployment and after intervention, cross-tabulated against whether the student named the error at item 5. **The cross-tabulation is the claim and it is uncomfortable for the design**: if students who predicted the error commit it at the same rate as students who did not, then predicting a failure and avoiding it are unrelated, and the entire sealed-prediction instrument measures something other than what the [Copilot Practice Standard](/wiki/program/12-Copilot-Practice-Standard.md) claims for it. **That would be a finding about the standard and not about this day**, and this is the first occasion in the programme on which the same student's prediction and performance on the same failure can be paired.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: More than half of students will write a floor at item 2, and fewer than half of those will hold it against B.
predictions.instrument: item 2 paired with element 7 and with the phase 4 walk-away answer, coded for whether the floor was written, whether it was reached, and whether it moved. **The pairing is the claim.** If floors are written and held at similar rates, the design's central hypothesis at phase 6 point 2 — that writing it before the room is what determines holding it — is unsupported and the element is a formality.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: More than a third of students will agree a scope with A that B declines to resource, and **fewer than half of those will tell A before the defence.**
predictions.instrument: the two encounter records paired, coded for the A-agreed-B-refused condition and for whether A was informed. **The second figure is the day's most important measurement**, and if it is high the occasion's central difficulty is not a difficulty and phase 3's fixed order can be relaxed.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At element 4, more than half of out-of-scope items will name an assignee who has not been told, and the modal excluded item will be one whose assignment would have resolved the resource constraint.
predictions.instrument: element 4 entries coded for assignee presence and for whether the assignee was informed, cross-tabulated against the B encounter's refusal grounds. **The cross-tabulation is the claim**: if excluded items and refused resources are unrelated, §1's account of why exclusions matter is wrong and element 4 is bookkeeping.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: In the phase 5 part-three comparison, students' [S039](/wiki/seminars/S039.md) absent-party results will not predict their element 2 quality at a two-year gap.
predictions.instrument: the S039 phase 7 outcome against element 2's completeness, coded by the assessors in the sealed field. **This is the prediction the design expects to lose and reports anyway**, because [WP-039](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-039.md) §6 asserted that day was this one's rehearsal, and a rehearsal that does not predict is a claim about the retention schedule that has failed rather than a claim about the students.

predictions.label: Prediction 5.
predictions.claim: At item 5, **more than three-quarters will predict that the agent answers the quota question completely, and fewer than a fifth will state that it cannot reach whether the grantor will agree.** Across the module, **the second rate will not rise from S081 to S085.**
predictions.instrument: item 5 coded on two axes at each of the module's five days, reported as a five-point series per cohort. **The second clause is the claim and it is the module's only test of whether frontier calibration is learnable within a module rather than merely measurable.** A rising series means the cohort is acquiring a boundary; a flat one means the design is taking five readings of a fixed disposition and reporting them as a trajectory, which is the failure instrumentation rule 9 exists to name. **The series is one cohort, one substrate, five staff-chosen tasks, and it is reported with that sampling attached** per instrumentation rule 3; it describes these five days and not the agent.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 4, the cohort's median estimate of the proportion of their component knowledge that is written down will be substantially higher than the proportion of step 3's enumerated items that turn out to have any existing written home.
predictions.instrument: item 4 fractions against a coding of step 3 entries for pre-existing documentation. **If the two agree, the day's premise is wrong for this cohort** and the module's opening claim should be rewritten as a claim about organisations rather than about individuals.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: More than half of groups will rank H1 above H4 before the outcome records are supplied, and the most common justification will appeal to coverage rather than to any of the three capabilities.
predictions.instrument: phase 3 rankings with their written justifications, coded for the criterion appealed to. **The justification is the claim**, not the ranking: a group that ranks H1 first on a capability argument has reasoned well and been wrong, which is a different finding from ranking on volume.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: Step 2's predictions will not be systematically over-confident in magnitude — because point 7 has just been taught — **and will be systematically wrong in composition**: students will predict the receiver will fail on the *diagnose* capability and the receiver will in fact fail on *change*.
predictions.instrument: step 6's item-by-item gap, coded by capability, with the aggregate direction reported separately from the composition. **The composition is the prediction that survives §8 objection 1's confound**, because point 7 tells students that they over-predict and tells them nothing about which capability travels worst.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: Phase 7 triads will classify divergences as context gaps more often than as artefact gaps, and the same divergence classes will appear as artefact gaps in the step 5 stranger reconstructions.
predictions.instrument: the phase 7 classification set against the step 6 record, matched by divergence class. **If this holds it is direct evidence for §8 objection 2's concession** — that a peer is the wrong second reader — and it is reported with the receiver dose attached in both cases.

predictions.label: Prediction 5 — the practical turn's own instrument, per §8 objection 3.
predictions.claim: Students whose step 4 change is concentrated in the infrastructure declaration rather than in code, tests and names will show a **smaller** operate-capability gap at step 6 and **no smaller** change-capability gap, and will be over-represented among the students whose receiver could complete the nominated operation and could not name a change they would be afraid to make.
predictions.instrument: the step 4 diff, coded by what it touched, against the step 6 gap by capability and against the receiver's third reconstruction answer. **If the correlation is absent, objection 3 is wrong and the exclusion from assessment was sufficient.** If it is present, the day has an optimisation target it did not intend, and the response is to move the nominated operation out of phase 5 and leave it in phase 3, where its insufficiency is staged rather than merely stated.

predictions.label: Prediction 6 — the frontier item.
predictions.claim: A large majority of item 7 sealed predictions will state that the agent will invent or mis-state a procedural step, and a small minority will name the specific class — a value that resolves only in the author's environment, a resource the declaration does not contain, a permission the receiver does not hold.
predictions.instrument: item 7 responses coded for generic-versus-specific failure identification, against what each student's agent actually produced at step 4. **The gap between the two rates is the day's frontier-calibration measure and is read by next year's cohort** through the [Durable and Perishable Register](/wiki/program/09-Durable-and-Perishable-Register.md), per instrumentation rule 9. If the specific rate is high, the cohort's model of the agent on handover material is better than the design assumes and phase 6's agent case is redundant.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At phase 1, the ratio between the number of evidence items students list at item 2 and the number they can give an error direction for at item 3 will be large, and the items that survive will be disproportionately tests rather than operational records.
predictions.instrument: items 2 and 3 paired per student, with surviving items coded by evidence kind. **The composition is the claim**: if operational records survive as often as tests, the cohort holds a better model of production evidence than the day assumes and phase 4 point 3 is over-taught.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: A majority of groups will rank C1 or C2 above C4 before the outcome is supplied, and the justifications will appeal to completeness or traceability rather than to any of the four boundaries.
predictions.instrument: phase 3 rankings with justifications coded for the criterion appealed to. **If the justifications appeal to boundaries and the ranking still favours breadth, the day's problem is not the belief it thinks it is**, and point 1 needs rewriting as an argument about evidence supply rather than about claim strength.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At step 5, adversary assumptions will be the least populated of the three sets and operator assumptions the least *owned* — that is, students will write operator assumptions and leave them with no responsible party more often than any other kind.
predictions.instrument: step 5 assumption sets coded by kind and by ownership, reported as two separate distributions. **The two failures are different and the design predicts different ones for different sets**, which is what makes this falsifiable rather than a general prediction that assumptions are hard.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At phase 7, partners will more often identify a use the claim accidentally covers than an assumption likely to fail first, and the gap will be large.
predictions.instrument: phase 7's three answers coded for correctness against the author's adjudication. **If assumptions are identified more readily, the boundary is not the hard part for this cohort** and the day's emphasis is misplaced; the design would then move phase 5's unsupported step from 1 to 5.

predictions.label: Prediction 5 — the practical turn's own instrument, per §8 objection 3.
predictions.claim: The evidence surviving into step 2 will be **more heavily weighted toward test and gate artefacts, and less toward operator and organisational accounts, than the same students' phase 1 item 2 lists were** — that is, the composition will shift between the pretest and the artefact, in the direction the reproducibility column rewards.
predictions.instrument: item 2 lists and step 2 lists coded by evidence kind, paired per student, reported as a composition shift rather than as a count. **If there is no shift, objection 3 is wrong and the admissibility of *not reproducible* was sufficient.** If the shift is large, the day has bought checkability at the price of the assumption class point 5 exists to install, and the response is to move the bundle out of the assessed artefact and into phase 3 only.

predictions.label: Prediction 6 — the frontier item.
predictions.claim: A large majority of item 8 sealed predictions will state that the agent's query will run and mislead, and a small minority will name the mechanism — a table that is being replaced, a filter that silently excludes, a window shorter than the claim.
predictions.instrument: item 8 responses coded for generic-versus-specific identification against what each student's agent produced at step 3. **The gap between the two rates is the day's frontier-calibration measure**, its reader is next year's cohort, and a high specific rate would mean phase 6's agent case is redundant for this cohort.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 3, self-protection will be the least-cited reason for an omission and, at phase 7, partners will identify the author's position as the beneficiary of the omission more often than authors did.
predictions.instrument: item 3 reasons coded into the four categories, set against phase 7's condition-two classifications for the same items. **The gap is the claim**, not either figure alone: the design predicts that authors and readers of the same omission disagree systematically about who it served.

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: More than a third of groups will rank R2 first before the outcome is supplied, and the justification will appeal to usability.
predictions.instrument: phase 3 rankings with justifications coded. **This is the prediction the day depends on**: if the room spots R2's omission unprompted, the implicating case does not implicate and phase 4 point 3 is being taught to a room that already holds it.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At phase 8, the cohort's item 4 positions will have moved from their week-thirteen [S013](/wiki/seminars/S013.md) positions in the direction of a stricter standard, and the movement will be larger for students whose S013 position was permissive.
predictions.instrument: the [S013](/wiki/seminars/S013.md) aggregate against item 4, coded for strictness and paired per student where the records permit. **No movement is the informative result** and is the reading [WP-013](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-013.md) §9 prediction 4 specified: it would indicate that neither [S013](/wiki/seminars/S013.md) nor this day changed anything, and that a two-year loop bought the programme nothing.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: At step 5, the condition that most often triggers an item's return to the statement will be counterfactual disclosure rather than recoverability, and the returned items will be disproportionately those the author's item 3 reason coded as *uncertainty*.
predictions.instrument: step 5 movements coded by triggering condition and matched to item 3 reasons. **If recoverability dominates instead, the day's third condition is doing no work** and the framework reduces to [S065](/wiki/seminars/S065.md)'s pair with better wording, which would mean this whitepaper's central claim to have advanced the question is false.

predictions.label: Prediction 5 — the practical turn's own, per §8 objection 3.
predictions.claim: The inherited-guarantee heading will be the **longest** of the five in the step 2 enumerations and the **shortest-lived** in the step 3 statements — that is, students will enumerate many inherited guarantees and carry almost none of them through, and the step 5 audit will rarely mark any of them decision-changing.
predictions.instrument: step 2 entries and step 3 survivals coded by heading, with the step 5 condition-three answers for the inherited-guarantee items reported separately. **If that pattern holds, point 10 has been received as a recording exercise and objection 3 is correct**, and the response is the reordering the objection names. **If inherited guarantees are marked decision-changing at the same rate as the other four headings, the platform content has been integrated into the ethics rather than appended to it**, which is what the design intends and has not demonstrated.

predictions.label: Prediction 6 — the frontier item.
predictions.claim: A large majority of item 8 sealed predictions will name a *risk* as the thing the agent will drop, and a small minority will name a *qualification* — a horizon, a confidence, an interval.
predictions.instrument: item 8 responses coded by omission class against what each student's agent actually dropped, with the two distributions reported side by side. **The design predicts that the observed distribution is dominated by qualifications and the predicted distribution by risks**, which would mean the cohort's model of the agent is about content and the agent's actual selection is about form — a frontier finding the phase 6 case states and this instrument would measure. Its reader is next year's cohort.

predictions.label: Prediction 1.
predictions.claim: At item 3, a majority of students will write *nothing* for what the receiving party must do, and at step 2 the same students will produce at least two receiver obligations each.
predictions.instrument: item 3 coded binary against the per-student obligation count. **If the item 3 rate is low, phase 3's payload is not defeating a belief this cohort holds** and W4's staging is spending forty-five minutes on a point already made by [S039](/wiki/seminars/S039.md).

predictions.label: Prediction 2.
predictions.claim: At item 4, the modal cold resolution of the contradiction will be to retreat to a function name, not to name a successor, and students who retreat will be disproportionately those who wrote strong [S069](/wiki/seminars/S069.md) arrangements.
predictions.instrument: item 4 answers coded into three categories — function, successor, both — and matched against [S069](/wiki/seminars/S069.md) specification outcomes where records permit. **The correlation is the claim**: it would indicate that the students who best internalised the earlier rule are the ones the contradiction damages most, which is what a rule taught without its scope does.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: At phase 7, partners will name an unusable ownership entry less often than they name a missing item, and the ownership-entry rate will be lower than it would be for an artefact in plain named-person form.
predictions.instrument: the phase 7 third answer, with a comparison arm supplied by the four phase 3 artefacts read under the same protocol on day 3 of the between-day set. **This is the design's only test of whether slot-and-occupant helps a reader**, it is weak, and §8 objection 1 states why a better one was declined.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: More than a third of receiving parties will decline at least one obligation at step 6, and the most commonly declined class will be recurring checks rather than one-off notifications.
predictions.instrument: step 6 records coded by obligation class. **If almost nothing is declined, the negotiation is ceremonial** — either the obligations were written to be acceptable, which the assessors can see in the table, or the receiving party does not believe they will be held to them, which is worse and is not visible in the artefact at all.

predictions.label: Prediction 5 — the practical turn's own, per §8 objection 3.
predictions.claim: At step 8, the modal number of *enforces more* entries will be **zero** on first submission and non-zero after the assessors' query, and the settings most often unmentioned in the warranty will be the unmanage action and the excluded-principal list.
predictions.instrument: reconciliation tables at submission and after adjudication, coded by setting. **The prediction is that students write warranties about what they intend to guarantee and stacks about what they intend to prevent, and never notice the third category** — what the mechanism does that nobody promised. If *enforces more* is populated on first submission, the reconciliation is doing less work than the design claims and step 8 could be shortened to a declaration without a table.

predictions.label: Prediction 6 — the frontier item.
predictions.claim: A large majority of item 8 sealed predictions will name a **deny setting** as the term the agent will choose for them, and a small minority will name the **unmanage action**.
predictions.instrument: item 8 responses coded by setting against the settings the agent actually supplied at step 8. **The design predicts that the room's attention is on protection and the agent's most consequential choice is about destruction**, which is the phase 6 case's mechanism and would be, if it holds, a frontier finding about where a room looks when it reviews generated infrastructure. Its reader is next year's cohort, through the [Durable and Perishable Register](/wiki/program/09-Durable-and-Perishable-Register.md).

predictions.label: Prediction 1 — about the programme as a whole, and the one a cohort's outcomes would falsify most directly.
predictions.claim: **Fewer than half the cohort will reach 3b on all three activities, and EA-3 will be the lowest of the three for a majority of students.**
predictions.instrument: the three level distributions from this day, set against the exit determinations made by ME390, PE390, CAP390 and SG390. **If EA-3 is not the weakest, the programme's central diagnosis is wrong** — the [Programme Charter](/wiki/program/00-Program-Charter.md) exists because graduates "can measure, and cannot say what the measurement licenses," and EA-3 is the direct test of that claim. A cohort strong at EA-3 and weak at EA-1 would mean the programme identified the wrong binding constraint and rebuilt a curriculum around it.

predictions.label: Prediction 1b — the same prediction from the other side, and the sharper falsifier.
predictions.claim: **A cohort that reaches 3b on all three activities at a high rate falsifies the programme's exit target rather than vindicating its teaching.** The target was set at 3b because three years is short and [S070](/wiki/seminars/S070.md) expects 2b–3a with 3b rare; a cohort clearing it comfortably means either the assessors converged on the target because it was published, which rater discipline rule 4 predicts and rule 2 is designed to detect, or the target was set below what the design achieves.
predictions.instrument: the three distributions against assessor divergence rates and against the independent-before-deliberation records. **The design commits in advance to reading a high pass rate as a question about the occasion before reading it as a result about the students.**

predictions.label: Prediction 2 — the instrumentation prediction from §8 objection 2.
predictions.claim: **At the end of the first cohort, fewer than one in ten of the §9 predictions written across the ninety whitepapers will have been measured against cohort data, and the ones that were will be disproportionately those measurable inside a single seminar day.**
predictions.instrument: an audit of the whitepaper corpus against the collected data, conducted before the second offering, reporting the count measured, the count measurable-but-unmeasured, and the count that turned out to be unmeasurable as written. **If most are measured, §8 objection 2 is wrong and the programme is better instrumented than its own closing paper believes.** The composition is as informative as the count: a skew toward within-day instruments would confirm that the design's long-horizon apparatus is the part that does not survive contact with capacity.

predictions.label: Prediction 3.
predictions.claim: **Fewer than half of students will correctly identify, at item 4, the activity on which they are judged worst.**
predictions.instrument: item 4 against the three awarded levels, with ties resolved by the assessors' narratives. **This is the programme's terminal calibration measure**, and it is the same construction phase 8 has run every week for three years, asked one last time about the students themselves rather than about their material.

predictions.label: Prediction 4.
predictions.claim: **The phase 7 participation rate will be lower than any prior error clinic in the programme, and the [S010](/wiki/seminars/S010.md) instrument's twelfth administration will not register the drop.**
predictions.instrument: the participation rate recorded by the module lead against the twelve-point series. **This is the prediction the design most needs to be wrong about.** If the behaviour and the instrument diverge, the programme's psychological-safety claim has been resting for three years on a self-report that a room will complete favourably while declining to speak — and the pre-committed response, stated in the day's rule-6 block, is to treat the behaviour as the finding and replace the instrument.

predictions.label: Prediction 5 — about the dependency risk specifically, and the one this programme has the least right to be confident about.
predictions.claim: **Across the three unassisted occasions, the cohort's median completion of the bounded task will not fall, and the *spread* will widen** — that is, the provision will show no cohort-level decline in unassisted construction and a growing minority for whom the gap between assisted and unassisted work is large.
predictions.instrument: the three-point series in aggregate, reported as median and spread, with the phase 1b completion, look-up and stopping records coded. **Three outcomes and the design's response to each is pre-committed here, because instrumentation rule 4 requires it and because a prediction about the programme's own safeguard must not be allowed to resolve after the fact.** - **Median falls across the three points.** The dependency risk is real at cohort level, three occasions detected it, and the fading schedule in the [Module Map](/wiki/program/07-Module-Map.md) is the thing that changes — not the students, and not the tool policy. - **Median holds and spread widens.** The predicted result. It means the risk is real for a subset and invisible in any aggregate, which is the worst case for a detector with three points and no per-student resolution, and the response is to increase the number of occasions rather than their difficulty. - **Median holds and spread does not widen.** The most comfortable result and the one to distrust hardest, because **it is exactly what a task too easy to discriminate would produce.** The response is to check the task before believing the finding, and the design commits to that ordering in advance so that a null result cannot be read as reassurance. **No effect size is asserted for any of the three, and the programme has no comparison group, no pre-turn cohort and no instrument capable of separating a change in capability from a change in the task.** §3.2's second scope statement bounds the reading, and this prediction is stated as a direction and a shape rather than as a magnitude for that reason.

predictions.label: Prediction 6 — about the practical turn, per §8 objection 5.
predictions.claim: **The cohort's specific-naming rate on the sealed Copilot prediction will rise across the ninety-day series, and the rise will be concentrated in the second and third years rather than distributed evenly.**
predictions.instrument: the ninety-day frontier map's two rates, plotted by day, with the generic rate reported separately. **If the specific rate is flat, the turn's phase 1 addition has been measuring an attitude toward the tool rather than a model of it, and the correct response is to withdraw the sealed item rather than to tighten it.** If the specific rate rises and phase 2's durable-item performance falls, §8 objection 5's second candidate is the true one and the turn has traded understanding for familiarity — in which case the platform anchors stay, because the validity argument survives, and the phase 4 platform points shrink to one per day.

teaching_moves.text: Predict: will your answer to item 3 match the machine's count? Item 4 is the calibration item. Students commit to a yes or no, and the reveal comes in phase 4. **The Copilot prediction, sealed.** A fifth item, answered before phase 3:

teaching_moves.text: The agent will be given the same reference card and asked to trace the same sequence. **Will its trace be correct — and if it is wrong, at which step, and how will you be able to tell?** The third clause is the item. Item 5 is bound to phase 1 by instrumentation rule 8: asked after phase 3 it would measure recall of what phase 3 had already displayed. ---

teaching_moves.text: Predict: how many of items 1–5 did you get right? **The Copilot prediction, sealed.** A seventh item:

teaching_moves.text: The agent will be asked items 1 to 5 as questions, and then asked to *write the code* that each item is about. **Will its answers and its code agree — and if they diverge, on which item, and in which direction?** The direction clause is the item. Most students who consider the question at all predict that the code will be better than the prose, because code is the thing the tool is for. **Warrant.** Every item is a case where the intuitive answer is confidently wrong. The prediction in item 6 makes the overconfidence measurable rather than merely asserted. Item 7 extends the same instrument to the tool and is sealed at phase 1 per instrumentation rule 8. ---

teaching_moves.text: Predict: will the room agree with you? Item 3 is the calibration item. The room does not agree, and the disagreement is the day's opening fact. **The Copilot prediction, sealed.** A fourth item:
teaching_moves.day_title: S004 · Proof as an Act of Communication
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Copilot as a proof-checking adversary; Learn MCP for definition grounding

teaching_moves.text: The agent will be shown the same three arguments and asked, for each, whether it would accept it from a colleague. **How many will it reject — and will it identify the gap in argument C?** Most students predict that the tool will find C's gap, on the ground that finding gaps is a mechanical task and mechanical tasks are what tools are for. Argument C reaches a true conclusion, and that is the property the prediction fails to account for. **Warrant.** Pretesting on untaught material, with a generation demand. The disagreement establishes, empirically and in the first half hour, that sufficiency is reader-relative — which is the day's thesis, arrived at rather than announced. Item 4 is sealed at phase 1 per instrumentation rule 8. ---

teaching_moves.text: A loop is given. State what is true after every iteration. (Most students state what is true *at the end*, which is a different and weaker claim.)

teaching_moves.platform_anchor: GitHub Copilot agent mode; custom instructions as executable specification · Copilot as a proof-checking adversary

teaching_moves.text: An inductive argument is given with a subtly wrong base case. Is the conclusion true?

teaching_moves.text: A property is stated that holds for the first thousand inputs. Does it hold for all?

teaching_moves.text: Predict: will your answer to item 1 be the property the instructor has in mind? **The Copilot prediction, sealed.** A fifth item:
teaching_moves.day_title: S005 · Induction and the Machine That Runs Forever
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: GitHub Copilot agent mode; custom instructions as executable specification · Copilot as a proof-checking adversary

teaching_moves.text: The agent will be shown four loops with four candidate properties and asked, for each, whether the property is an invariant. **How many will it get right — and will its errors be in the same places as yours?** The second clause is the item, and it is the last Copilot prediction of the module because it is the one the module has been building toward. Four days of predictions have asked *where will the tool be wrong*. This one asks **whether being right yourself will tell you.** **Warrant.** Item 1 is the day's core skill, pretested before instruction; the characteristic error — confusing the postcondition with the invariant — appears immediately and is diagnostic. Item 2 separates a true conclusion from a warranted one, retrieving S004 phase 1's argument C. Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 per instrumentation rule 8, and is the module's terminal frontier item. ---

teaching_moves.text: **Sealed Copilot prediction.** The same forty lines will be given to Copilot in agent mode, with the wording of item 1 as the prompt. Write down now, and seal it: what will the agent produce, and **where will it be wrong**? A prediction that says only "it will do well" or "it will miss things" does not count; name the property you think it will miss, or the kind of property it will invent. Item 3 is the transfer probe and it is the day's most important measurement — not of the students, but of the design. Item 4 is calibration, and students overestimate. Item 5 is sealed with the rest and opened at phase 8; its cohort accuracy is this day's contribution to the programme's running frontier map, and the design expects the *where will it be wrong* half to be much weaker than the *what will it do* half. **Warrant.** Pretesting with a generation demand on untaught material. Item 3 tests whether S005's technique survived a change of setting after two days; the result is recorded as a design finding. Item 5 is administered before phase 4 and may not migrate later, per instrumentation rule 8: a frontier prediction made after the frontier has been shown measures recall. ---

teaching_moves.text: **Sealed Copilot prediction.** The same function will be handed to Copilot in agent mode with the instruction *split this*. Write down now, and seal it: what seams will the agent draw, and **where will its decomposition be wrong**? Name the change you think it will make expensive. Item 3 is the day's central move, asked before any instruction, and most students cannot answer it. That inability is the pretest's result. Item 5 is opened at phase 8; the design expects the room to predict the agent's seams accurately and its costs badly, which is the same failure item 3 exposes in their own work. **Warrant.** Pretesting with generation. Item 3 establishes, before instruction, that students have a decomposition instinct and no cost model — which is the day's thesis produced by the students rather than asserted at them. teaching_moves.text: **Sealed Copilot prediction.** Later today you will give an agent a research task over the Microsoft Learn documentation with a stopping condition you write yourself. teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly hand this exact request to the agent and ask it to implement it. Write down what it will produce — and **say whether it will tell you the request cannot be satisfied, at what point, and in what words.** Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 3 is collected and returned at phase 8. Item 4's answers are usually long. **Item 5's answers are usually wrong in one direction:** the design's expectation is that a substantial number of students predict a refusal or a caveat, and that the agent produces neither. **Warrant.** Pretesting on the professional act before the technical instruction, so that the day's later draft can be compared against an untutored one written by the same student. Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8, and it is the day's cheapest demonstration that the duty cannot be delegated: a student who predicted the agent would flag the impossibility, and finds it did not, has learned who is responsible without being told. ---

teaching_moves.label: Request 1 — genuinely impossible as asked.
teaching_moves.text: *"Make the `category` field filterable so support can filter by product line."* An existing field's attributes are not modifiable. The change requires dropping the index and rebuilding it from source.
teaching_moves.day_title: S024 · Intractability and the Duty to Say So
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search — index schema immutability and the reranker's candidate window

teaching_moves.label: Request 2 — genuinely impossible as asked.
teaching_moves.text: *"Turn on semantic reranking so we stop missing this document."* The reranker reorders the candidate set it is given; it does not re-run the query over the corpus. A document that did not enter the first stage's candidate set cannot be recovered by reranking it, and the document in this request did not.
teaching_moves.day_title: S024 · Intractability and the Duty to Say So
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search — index schema immutability and the reranker's candidate window

teaching_moves.label: Request 3 — looks impossible and is not.
teaching_moves.text: *"We need the description field returned in results."* It is a change to an existing field, which sounds like request 1 and is not: **setting a field's retrievability is on the short list of modifications that require no rebuild.** The instance class is restricted in a way that makes it easy, and only reading the list tells you so.
teaching_moves.day_title: S024 · Intractability and the Duty to Say So
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search — index schema immutability and the reranker's candidate window

teaching_moves.label: Request 4 — looks impossible and is not, once you ask what was wanted.
teaching_moves.text: *"We need results grouped by category."* Grouping needs a facetable field and the existing one cannot become facetable. But **a new field can be added to an index with no rebuild at all**, carrying the same value, facetable from birth; existing documents hold nothing in it until they are reindexed. The requester wanted grouping. They did not want that particular field.
teaching_moves.day_title: S024 · Intractability and the Duty to Say So
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search — index schema immutability and the reranker's candidate window

teaching_moves.label: Request 5 — impossible as asked, with an approximation the requester would accept entirely.
teaching_moves.text: *"The rebuild would take search down and we cannot have downtime."* The rebuild is real and it is required. The downtime is not: an index alias lets a replacement index be built alongside the original and swapped in **without changing application code.**
teaching_moves.day_title: S024 · Intractability and the Duty to Say So
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search — index schema immutability and the reranker's candidate window

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent, through the Foundry MCP Server, to *evaluate this model and tell me whether it is good enough to ship*. Write down what it will produce, and **name the one thing it will get wrong**. Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 3 is the day's move. Item 4's answer is lower, and predicting it is not the same as being able to say why. Item 5's prompt is deliberately the prompt a student would actually write, and it contains a question the agent cannot answer — *good enough* is a property of a decision, not of a model. The design's expectation is that a majority predict the agent will produce an evaluation run and a number, and that a minority predict it will **answer the shipping question anyway**, which is the failure that matters. **Warrant.** Pretesting on a real evaluation whose construction is disclosed at item 2. The construction contains a leak that most students do not identify even when shown it. Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8: an instrument administered after its answer has been taught measures recall. ---

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to *find me the best-performing configuration for this task.* Write down what it will produce, and **name the one thing it will get wrong**. teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent, in these words, to *build us an evaluator for this assistant*. teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to *validate our evaluation criterion*. Write down what it will produce, and **name the one thing it will get wrong**. Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 4's answer is no. No individual adjustment broke it and the sequence did. Item 5's expectation is that the agent will produce a genuinely competent validation — a held-out set, a run, a report — and will validate the version currently registered against the judgement of the person who registered it, which is the one check the criterion cannot fail. The absence of a culprit is the day's content and is discovered rather than asserted. Item 5 is administered here and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8. ---

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to *review the evaluator you built at S046 and the check you built at S047, and tell you what is wrong with them.* Write down what it will flag, **what it will not flag, and which of those two lists is longer**. Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 2's movement is substantial and is not random with respect to position. Item 5 is the day's contribution to the running frontier map and the sharpest one the programme takes. The agent wrote most of both artefacts. The design's expectation is that it will produce a fluent, correct, useful review of the things it can see — schema, coverage, edge cases — and will not raise the defect it introduced, because the reasoning that produced the defect is the reasoning being asked to find it. **Warrant.** Pretesting with a re-presentation reveal. Same judge, same outputs, different order, different scores — which is unarguable and requires no framework to see. Item 5 is administered here and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8, and its two-list form is deliberate: predicting that a self-review misses things is easy, and predicting the ratio is the measure. ---

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to create a search index over the substrate corpus and load it, using nothing but a description of the corpus. Write down what it will produce — the field attributes, the analyser, the scoring configuration — and **name the one thing it will get wrong.** Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 1's ordering is deliberate — mark first, articulate second — because the rule students write is a reconstruction and the day needs them to see that. Item 5 is the day's contribution to the running frontier map. The design's expectation is that most students will predict the agent gets a *parameter* wrong and few will predict that it gets a *field attribute* wrong — and the field attributes are what determine whether anything is scored at all, because **only fields marked searchable participate in scoring and only fields marked retrievable come back.** **Construction rule.** The twelve queries are **selected against [S051](/wiki/seminars/S051.md)'s item 1 grouping distribution**, which measured whether the cohort's unaided notion of similarity is behavioural or semantic. If the cohort's groupings clustered on E3, the set is weighted toward queries whose clicked result is not the correct one and whose correct answer is found by exact rare-term match. If they clustered on E2, the set is weighted toward queries where paraphrase similarity retrieves a fluent wrong document and the rare term retrieves the right one. **In both branches the majority intuition is the one the set defeats**, and which branch runs is decided from the S051 data before the day is delivered. **Warrant.** Pretesting on a task students can perform, with the articulation deliberately placed after the performance. The construction rule is this day's discharge of the obligation [S051](/wiki/seminars/S051.md) placed on it under instrumentation rule 6: the response to that measurement is a change in what phase 1 contains, not a mention of it. **Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8: an instrument administered after its answer has been taught measures recall.** ---

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to build you a release gate: a Foundry evaluation run, wired into a pipeline, that decides whether a change may ship. The design's expectation is that most students will predict the agent gets an evaluator or a data mapping wrong, and that few will predict what it actually does — which is to produce a correct, runnable, well-structured pipeline **that accepts the default threshold, accepts the default split, and contains no failure condition**, because none of those is an error and all three are decisions. **Warrant.** Pretesting on an artefact the students already trust, with the record in front of them. Item 3 is constructed so that both available answers are wrong in interesting ways — *the changes were good* and *the gate is broken* are each half of a claim about a gate whose false-block rate has never been measured. Item 2's placement before phase 4 is deliberate and is defended in [WP-066](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-066.md) §8, which concedes that the placement does not protect the assessed version of the same question. Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8: an instrument administered after its answer has been taught measures recall. ---

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to add a tool to your capability and to make sure it cannot be used for one named purpose. **Write down what it will produce, and name the one thing it will get wrong.** Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 1 is the two-directional documentation gap [WP-034](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-034.md) §9 carried forward as the cohort's contract-reading baseline, re-probed here at four quarters; the S034 rate is the baseline this one is read against and both are reported together at phase 8. Item 4 is the day's discriminator, and the room's numbers are low. **Item 5 is the day's contribution to the running frontier map**, and the design's expectation is that most students predict the prohibition will be expressed in the tool's description — which is where a helpful assistant would put it, and which is the one place in the surface that constrains nothing. **Warrant.** Pretesting on a real tool with its real specification, so that item 1 measures a capability rather than a memory and can be compared against the same student's [S034](/wiki/seminars/S034.md) result. Item 2's *where did it get that idea* clause is what turns a diagnosis into the day's mechanism: the answer is almost always the tool's name. Item 3 requires a student to locate a transition they have no vocabulary for, which is what makes the phase 4 definition land as a name for something they have already found. Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8; it is the same shape as [S071](/wiki/seminars/S071.md) item 5 one construct further out, and the movement between the two is reported at phase 8. ---
teaching_moves.day_title: S073 · Protocols, Tools and the Boundary of Trust
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: MCP — tool annotations as hints, `require_approval`, `allowed_tools`

teaching_moves.label: T1
teaching_moves.text: a narrow typed schema, a permission scoped to a single record, no free-text field anywhere in the surface, annotated read-only.
teaching_moves.day_title: S073 · Protocols, Tools and the Boundary of Trust
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: MCP — tool annotations as hints, `require_approval`, `allowed_tools`

teaching_moves.label: T2
teaching_moves.text: a broad schema with excellent documentation: complete, accurate, and explicit about what the tool must not be used for.
teaching_moves.day_title: S073 · Protocols, Tools and the Boundary of Trust
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: MCP — tool annotations as hints, `require_approval`, `allowed_tools`

teaching_moves.label: T3
teaching_moves.text: a tool whose returned value contains content authored by a third party — a document body, a ticket comment, a page fetched from elsewhere.
teaching_moves.day_title: S073 · Protocols, Tools and the Boundary of Trust
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: MCP — tool annotations as hints, `require_approval`, `allowed_tools`

teaching_moves.label: T4
teaching_moves.text: a tool that wraps another agent.
teaching_moves.day_title: S073 · Protocols, Tools and the Boundary of Trust
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: MCP — tool annotations as hints, `require_approval`, `allowed_tools`

teaching_moves.text: An agent run is supplied that produced a wrong result. **Every tool call in it returned success.** Where did it go wrong?
teaching_moves.day_title: S074 · Tool Failure Has Four Shapes
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — the five tool-call evaluators

teaching_moves.text: **Enumerate the outcomes a tool call can have.** Write the complete list.
teaching_moves.day_title: S074 · Tool Failure Has Four Shapes
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — the five tool-call evaluators

teaching_moves.text: Three more runs are supplied. All reported success, all were wrong, and all were wrong differently. **State what distinguishes them** — and, for each, **name who in that system would have been positioned to notice it, or state that nobody would.**
teaching_moves.day_title: S074 · Tool Failure Has Four Shapes
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — the five tool-call evaluators

teaching_moves.text: Predict: **of the four failures you will see today, how many would appear on a monitoring dashboard?**
teaching_moves.day_title: S074 · Tool Failure Has Four Shapes
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — the five tool-call evaluators

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** For two years you have watched this agent choose tools, supply arguments, execute them and use what came back. **Write down which of those four it gets wrong most often in your experience, and predict which one today's cases will show it is worst at.** Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 2 is the re-probe [WP-033](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-033.md) §9 carried here as the cohort's outcome-space baseline; the [S033](/wiki/seminars/S033.md) item 1 count is the figure this one is read against, and both are reported together at phase 8. **Item 3's second clause is the day's headline instrument administered before the day supplies its answer**, and phase 5 step 4 is the same question on the student's own system; the measure is the shift between them rather than either alone. Item 4's answer is two, and the room's median is four. **Item 5 is the day's contribution to the running frontier map, and it is the module's recursion made into a measurement.** The students' own instrument exhibits all four shapes; they have two years of experience of it; and the question is whether that experience has produced a usable model or an anecdote. The design's expectation is that the room names execution and input — the two it has seen reported — and that the two it cannot see are the two it has been living with. **Warrant.** Pretesting on runs whose failure is invisible in the artefact the room would normally consult, so that item 1 establishes the day's problem before any vocabulary exists. Item 2 is a genuine re-measurement rather than a recall check: [S033](/wiki/seminars/S033.md) asked the same question of a callee that was not a component producing plausible things, and whether four quarters and a module of agent material change the answer is the instrument's whole point. **Item 3's second clause was added after [WP-074](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-074.md) §8 found the day's headline instrument sitting downstream of the instruction that supplies its answer** — the third recorded instance of that pattern in this design — and it is what converts the step 4 measure from a recall check into a movement. Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8, and it is deliberately about the tool in the students' hands rather than about the substrate's, because the frontier map's whole subject is that instrument. ---
teaching_moves.day_title: S074 · Tool Failure Has Four Shapes
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — the five tool-call evaluators

teaching_moves.label: F1
teaching_moves.text: the system called a tool that succeeded and was not the tool the request needed. A neighbouring tool, plausibly named, with an overlapping surface.
teaching_moves.day_title: S074 · Tool Failure Has Four Shapes
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — the five tool-call evaluators

teaching_moves.label: F2
teaching_moves.text: the right tool, with arguments that encode a different question. The call was valid, the schema accepted it, the result is well-formed and is about something else.
teaching_moves.day_title: S074 · Tool Failure Has Four Shapes
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — the five tool-call evaluators

teaching_moves.label: F3
teaching_moves.text: the tool returned a stale value from a cache after its upstream dependency had been unavailable for two hours. The call reported success and the value was two hours old.
teaching_moves.day_title: S074 · Tool Failure Has Four Shapes
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — the five tool-call evaluators

teaching_moves.label: F4
teaching_moves.text: the tool returned the correct value and the system's next step used it wrongly: read a rate as a total.
teaching_moves.day_title: S074 · Tool Failure Has Four Shapes
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — the five tool-call evaluators

teaching_moves.text: An agent trajectory is supplied that reached the right answer. **Was it a good run?** State your criterion in one sentence — **and name one thing your criterion could not detect about this run.**
teaching_moves.day_title: S075 · Evaluating a Trajectory, Not an Answer
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — conversation split strategies and cloud evaluation

teaching_moves.text: **The same trajectory with every tool result removed**, leaving only the system's own stated reasoning. **Same question, same two parts.**
teaching_moves.day_title: S075 · Evaluating a Trajectory, Not an Answer
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — conversation split strategies and cloud evaluation

teaching_moves.text: A second trajectory reached the **wrong** answer by a path that is defensible at every step. A third reached the **right** answer by a path that is wrong at every step. **Which is the better system, and what would you need to decide?**
teaching_moves.day_title: S075 · Evaluating a Trajectory, Not an Answer
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — conversation split strategies and cloud evaluation

teaching_moves.text: Predict: **when a model judge scores these trajectories, which will it prefer** — the longer or the shorter, and the one that explains itself or the one that does not?
teaching_moves.day_title: S075 · Evaluating a Trajectory, Not an Answer
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — conversation split strategies and cloud evaluation

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to build an evaluation of your capability's task completion over last week's runs. **Write down what it will produce, and name the one thing it will get wrong.** Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 2 is the day's central finding administered before it is named, and it is the [WP-052](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-052.md) closure in its most direct form: **the stated reasoning is a produced output, not a record of the computation**, and a student whose judgement of the run does not move when the tool results are removed has been reading the narration. **Item 1's second clause is the day's headline instrument administered before phase 4 supplies its answer**; phase 5 step 7 is the same question about the student's own evaluation, and the measure is the movement. **Item 5 is the day's contribution to the running frontier map**, and it is deliberately the last of the module's five, because by now the room has a two-day-old habit of predicting that the agent will get a *limit* wrong. The design's expectation is that most students predict a coding error and that few predict the failure that actually matters — **that the evaluation will be correct, will run, will produce a number, and will answer a different question from the one asked**, because nothing in the request determines the unit and something has to. **Warrant.** Pretesting on an artefact the room will read as an explanation, with the removal at item 2 supplying the counter-evidence inside the same phase. Item 3 has no answer available from the trajectories alone and is the day's honest item: what a student needs is an intervention, which is point 3, and most of the room asks for more trajectories instead. Item 1's second clause is the pending elevation argued at [WP-074](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-074.md) §8 applied voluntarily on the day after it was argued, and [WP-075](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-075.md) §7 records it as a contingent reuse. Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8. ---
teaching_moves.day_title: S075 · Evaluating a Trajectory, Not an Answer
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — conversation split strategies and cloud evaluation

teaching_moves.label: E1 — outcome only.
teaching_moves.text: Did the run reach the requested end state? Binary, cheap, computed locally from the system's effects rather than from its record, with no judge and no API call.
teaching_moves.day_title: S075 · Evaluating a Trajectory, Not an Answer
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — conversation split strategies and cloud evaluation

teaching_moves.label: E2 — step level.
teaching_moves.text: Every step judged for whether it was the right next action, scoring each exchange independently with cumulative context. Rich, expensive, and requiring a criterion for *right next action* that nobody has written down.
teaching_moves.day_title: S075 · Evaluating a Trajectory, Not an Answer
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — conversation split strategies and cloud evaluation

teaching_moves.label: E3 — episode level.
teaching_moves.text: A rubric applied to the whole trajectory, including the system's stated reasoning, scored by a model judge.
teaching_moves.day_title: S075 · Evaluating a Trajectory, Not an Answer
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — conversation split strategies and cloud evaluation

teaching_moves.label: E4 — outcome plus replay.
teaching_moves.text: The run is re-executed from a recorded state with one step's tool result substituted, and the change in outcome is measured.
teaching_moves.day_title: S075 · Evaluating a Trajectory, Not an Answer
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Agent Framework — conversation split strategies and cloud evaluation

teaching_moves.text: **Mark every part of this context that somebody outside the engineering team can influence.** Mark it on the page.
teaching_moves.day_title: S076 · The Adversary Who Reads Your Prompt
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (user-prompt and document shields) and spotlighting, over a Foundry Agent Service component

teaching_moves.text: **For each thing you marked, name who can influence it and what it would cost them.**
teaching_moves.day_title: S076 · The Adversary Who Reads Your Prompt
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (user-prompt and document shields) and spotlighting, over a Foundry Agent Service component

teaching_moves.text: The agent's instructions say *never disclose the internal ticket identifier.* **Say how you would enforce that**, in one or two sentences.
teaching_moves.day_title: S076 · The Adversary Who Reads Your Prompt
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (user-prompt and document shields) and spotlighting, over a Foundry Agent Service component

teaching_moves.text: **Predict: what fraction of the printed context did you mark at item 1?**
teaching_moves.day_title: S076 · The Adversary Who Reads Your Prompt
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (user-prompt and document shields) and spotlighting, over a Foundry Agent Service component

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent, through the Foundry MCP Server, to *make this component resistant to prompt injection.* Write down what it will produce and **name the one thing it will get wrong.** Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 1 is the day's opening finding and needs no framework. Item 4 is asked separately from item 1 because the two answers diverge — students mark less than they then estimate they marked, which is the calibration result phase 8 reports. Item 3 is the day's payload administered before the day names it, and the answers are collected verbatim so that phase 8 can sort them into the three places of point 6. Item 5 is the day's contribution to the running frontier map. The design's expectation is that the agent will produce something real and configurable — a content filter, a delimiter convention, a hardened system prompt — and that it will produce a control at point 6's first place while describing it as a solution. **Predicting that the agent will get something wrong is easy; naming what is the measure**, and the two rates are reported separately. **Warrant.** Pretesting on a real assembled context with the answer physically present on the page, so that the phase 8 comparison is against a fact rather than against an opinion. Item 2 enforces [S044](/wiki/seminars/S044.md)'s actor requirement before the day can drift into hazards, which the module cannot assume is a habit after one prior day. Item 3 elicits the belief that enforcement belongs at the perimeter, which is the belief point 6 exists to correct, and it is elicited in the student's own words rather than as a multiple choice, because the sorting is the measurement. **Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 and may not migrate into phase 5, per instrumentation rule 8**, and it is deliberately the same question as item 3 asked of a different respondent — so the day measures the room's model of enforcement and the room's model of the agent's model of enforcement, and can report the gap. ---
teaching_moves.day_title: S076 · The Adversary Who Reads Your Prompt
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (user-prompt and document shields) and spotlighting, over a Foundry Agent Service component

teaching_moves.label: C1
teaching_moves.text: a user message containing an explicit instruction to disregard the agent's instructions. Crude, blocked by every filter the substrate has, and the case every student expects.
teaching_moves.day_title: S076 · The Adversary Who Reads Your Prompt
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (user-prompt and document shields) and spotlighting, over a Foundry Agent Service component

teaching_moves.label: C2
teaching_moves.text: a document from the substrate's own corpus, written by a real user two years ago in good faith. One sentence in it reads as an instruction only because of where the assembler places it. **The action C2's sentence asks for is selected against the schema reduction this cohort was least willing to make at [S073](/wiki/seminars/S073.md) step 4** — it is an action the room's own narrowest tool schema still admits, so that the best restriction the cohort was prepared to accept does not stop it.
teaching_moves.day_title: S076 · The Adversary Who Reads Your Prompt
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (user-prompt and document shields) and spotlighting, over a Foundry Agent Service component

teaching_moves.label: C3
teaching_moves.text: a tool's error string, quoted verbatim into the context. The text is controlled by the tool's upstream vendor and changes without notice.
teaching_moves.day_title: S076 · The Adversary Who Reads Your Prompt
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (user-prompt and document shields) and spotlighting, over a Foundry Agent Service component

teaching_moves.label: C4
teaching_moves.text: the agent's own output from three turns earlier, summarised back into the context by the orchestration layer built at [S072](/wiki/seminars/S072.md).
teaching_moves.day_title: S076 · The Adversary Who Reads Your Prompt
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Content Safety Prompt Shields (user-prompt and document shields) and spotlighting, over a Foundry Agent Service component

teaching_moves.text: **For each incident, say what the adversary did.**
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.text: **For each, name the signal that would have shown it, and say whether your own component emits that signal.**
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.text: **Which of the four would your [S068](/wiki/seminars/S068.md) detection design have caught?** Answer per incident.
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.text: **Predict: which of the four is cheapest for the adversary?**
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to *tell me whether my component is being attacked, from the evidence it has.* Write down what it will produce and **name the one thing it will get wrong.** Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 1 is phrased as it is on purpose, and phase 8 reads it back: **it assumes an adversary, and one of the four incidents does not have one.** Not a single student is expected to challenge the framing of the item, and the framing is the day's opening finding about the room rather than about the incidents. Item 2 is administered before instruction because the same question is asked again at step 3 after phase 4 has supplied the answer, and the design needs both readings rather than the second alone. **Item 5 is item 1's smuggled premise handed to a second respondent.** The prompt contains the same assumption the item does, and the design's expectation is that the agent will answer it — confidently, with a structure, and without objecting that the evidence cannot decide. A student who predicts that is predicting the day's payload from the agent's behaviour rather than from their own. **Warrant.** Pretesting on symptom records with the attribution withheld, so that the day's central discrimination is attempted cold. Item 3 joins the module to [M14](/wiki/modules/M14.md)'s detection work at the moment the student still believes their design covers the case, and its answer is the entry point for point 6. Item 1's smuggled premise is the pretest's payload and is the only item in the programme whose finding is that nobody objected to the question. **Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 per instrumentation rule 8** and is the day's contribution to the frontier map; it is constructed so that the agent's failure and the room's failure are the same failure, which is the cheapest available demonstration that a jagged frontier is not a property of the tool alone. ---
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.label: T1
teaching_moves.text: the index is poisoned through a user-contributed document. Evaluation scores are flat. One query class, not in the evaluation set, returns a document that was not previously retrievable.
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.label: T2
teaching_moves.text: extraction by querying. Several thousand individually ordinary requests, from a small number of principals, whose *joint* coverage of the embedding space is not ordinary at all.
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.label: T3
teaching_moves.text: exhaustion. A request shape chosen to maximise cost per unit of the adversary's own spend, arriving below every rate threshold the component has.
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.label: T4
teaching_moves.text: **the payload.** A record that looks exactly like T2 at the resolution supplied. It is a retry loop in an upstream client, released three days before the period began, written by a competent engineer, and there is no adversary anywhere in it.
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.label: T1 is executed.
teaching_moves.text: The group writes one document into the copy's index, reruns the evaluation set the student has maintained since [S049](/wiki/seminars/S049.md), and reads the scores. **They do not move.** Then they issue the trigger query and read what comes back. This is the day's cheapest and most important demonstration: point 2 is not that poisoning is possible but that **the evidence the room trusts most stays flat while it happens**, and no amount of stating that produces the effect of watching it.
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.label: T3 is executed.
teaching_moves.text: The group issues the T3 request shape against the copy behind an API Management token-limit policy of their own setting, and reads two things: what the gateway counted, and what the bill would have been. The gateway's own documentation is explicit that concurrent requests can temporarily exceed a configured token limit and that a streamed request's prompt tokens are always estimated — **so the meter that enforces the budget is itself approximate, and the size of the approximation is not published.**
teaching_moves.day_title: S077 · Poisoning, Extraction and Exhaustion
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Microsoft Defender for Cloud AI threat protection and its published alert catalogue · Azure API Management token-limit policy · the Foundry AI Red Teaming Agent

teaching_moves.text: **For each query, list the documents the system should return.** Work from the permission model on the page.
teaching_moves.day_title: S078 · Authorisation at Retrieval Time
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search document-level access control — the four approaches, the two-stage check, and index projections · Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI

teaching_moves.text: **Where in the pipeline would you enforce that?** Name the stage.
teaching_moves.day_title: S078 · Authorisation at Retrieval Time
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search document-level access control — the four approaches, the two-stage check, and index projections · Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI

teaching_moves.text: **A document's permissions changed yesterday. When does the answer change?** Give a time, not a mechanism.
teaching_moves.day_title: S078 · Authorisation at Retrieval Time
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search document-level access control — the four approaches, the two-stage check, and index projections · Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI

teaching_moves.text: **Predict: when you add the check, whose answers get worse, and by how much?**
teaching_moves.day_title: S078 · Authorisation at Retrieval Time
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search document-level access control — the four approaches, the two-stage check, and index projections · Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to *add document-level access control to this retrieval path.* Write down what it will produce and **name the one thing it will get wrong.** Sealed with items 1 to 4 and opened at phase 8. Item 4 is the day's payload administered before the day names it, and it is administered here rather than at phase 5 deliberately. **The design has recorded twice that it places its phase 5 instruments downstream of its own instruction** — opened at [WP-054](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-054.md) §8 and recorded as a second instance at [WP-066](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-066.md) §8 — and an instrument administered after its answer has been taught measures recall. Item 4 is measured against step 3's measurement, and both readings exist. Item 5 is the day's second payload. The design's expectation is a specific and testable one: **the agent will produce the string-filter approach**, because it is the generally available one with the most documentation and the most sample code, will implement it competently, and **will not say that the documentation calls it a workaround** or that the trust boundary now sits in the code it just wrote. The second expectation is sharper still — that whatever it produces will not project permission metadata onto chunks, because the chunking skillset and the access control are documented on different pages. **Warrant.** Pretesting against a real corpus and a real permission model with the correct answer derivable from the page, so that item 1 produces a graded result rather than an opinion. Item 3 asks for a duration because the students will supply a mechanism, and the substitution is the finding: staleness is a latency and the room does not have it as one. **Item 5 is sealed at phase 1 per instrumentation rule 8**, and it is the day's contribution to the frontier map. It is also the only Copilot prediction in the module with a documented right answer available before the day runs, which makes it the cohort's cleanest calibration datum — and the reason phase 8 reports the *named-the-failure* rate separately from the *predicted-a-failure* rate. ---
teaching_moves.day_title: S078 · Authorisation at Retrieval Time
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search document-level access control — the four approaches, the two-stage check, and index projections · Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI

teaching_moves.label: P1 — index time.
teaching_moves.text: A separate index per permission group. Correct results, no leakage, and an index count that grows with the permission structure rather than with the corpus. Staleness is a re-index.
teaching_moves.day_title: S078 · Authorisation at Retrieval Time
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search document-level access control — the four approaches, the two-stage check, and index projections · Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI

teaching_moves.label: P2 — query time.
teaching_moves.text: The permission predicate is pushed into the approximate index as a filter over metadata. Fast, and — this is [S058](/wiki/seminars/S058.md)'s material arriving where it was flagged to arrive — **its recall depends on the selectivity of the filter.** The more restricted the principal, the worse the search.
teaching_moves.day_title: S078 · Authorisation at Retrieval Time
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search document-level access control — the four approaches, the two-stage check, and index projections · Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI

teaching_moves.label: P3 — retrieval time.
teaching_moves.text: Post-filter the top *k*. Simplest, most widely deployed, and it **silently truncates**: a principal permitted four of the top ten receives four results and no indication that six were removed.
teaching_moves.day_title: S078 · Authorisation at Retrieval Time
teaching_moves.platform_anchor: Azure AI Search document-level access control — the four approaches, the two-stage check, and index projections · Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI

teaching_moves.label: P4 — answer time.
teaching_moves.text: Redact the generated answer. **The payload.**

teaching_moves.text: **Copilot prediction, sealed.** You will shortly ask the agent to *set up monitoring so I know if this component starts behaving differently.* Write down what it will produce and **name the one thing it will get wrong.** Sealed with items 1 to 5 and opened at phase 8. Items 2, 3 and 4 are administered here rather than at phase 5 and the reason is a design constraint rather than a preference. **The design has recorded twice that it places its phase 5 instruments downstream of its own instruction** — opened at [WP-054](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-054.md) §8 and recorded as a second instance at [WP-066](/wiki/whitepapers/WP-066.md) §8 — with the rule it would become already stated: *an instrument administered after its answer has been taught measures recall.* Item 4 in particular would be worthless at step 4, after phase 3's payload and phase 4 point 4 have supplied the answer. Both readings now exist and phase 8 reports the pair. **Item 6's expected failure is the day's whole subject arriving from a second direction.** The design's expectation is that the agent will produce a competent, complete-looking monitoring configuration — metrics, thresholds, an alert rule, possibly a sampled quality evaluation — and that **not one element of it will monitor whether the monitoring is still running.** A liveness property is not omitted because it is hard; it is omitted because nothing in the request or the documentation asks for it, and the agent answers the question it was given. **Warrant.** Pretesting against the cohort's own six-month record with the answers in the room and unopened. Item 2 asks for the student's belief about their own system before evidence, which is the only construction that measures whether they have been watching. Item 1 asks for a date because the drift series have no start and the students will supply one anyway, which is the finding point 1 consolidates. **Item 6 is sealed at phase 1 per instrumentation rule 8** and is the day's contribution to the frontier map. ---
